Faster Mixing for Triangulations via Transport Flows

Vedat Levi Alev ††thanks: University of Haifa — vedatalev@math.haifa.ac.il; Supported by the ISF Grant No. 721/2024 of Uriya A. First.    Daniel Frishberg ††thanks: California Polytechnic State University — dfrishbe@calpoly.edu    Michail Sarantis    Prasad Tetali ††thanks: Carnegie Mellon University — ptetali@cmu.edu; Supported in part by the NSF DMS-2151283 grant and Alexander M. Knaster Professorship.
August 24, 2026
Abstract

We prove an O~​(n2)\widetilde{O}(n^{2}) bound for the relaxation time and the log-Sobolev time (inverse log-Sobolev constant) of the classical triangulation flip chain on a convex (n+2)(n+2)-gon, implying a mixing time of O~​(n2)\widetilde{O}(n^{2}). The previous state of the art for the mixing time of this chain due to [EF23] [EF23] was O~​(n3)\widetilde{O}(n^{3}), while the best known lower bound on the mixing time due to [MRS97] [MRS97] is Ω⁡(n3/2)\Omega(n^{3/2}). Our relaxation time bound makes significant progress towards Aldous’ [Ald03] conjectured bound of Θ⁡(n3/2)\Theta(n^{3/2}) for the relaxation time.

We improve upon the analysis of [EF23] by further developing the framework of transport flows introduced in the work [Che+25] of [Che+25]. In this light, our results can be seen as a more efficient way of using combinatorial decompositions to obtain functional inequalities for Markov chains. We hope our ideas will find other applications in the future.

1 Introduction

Motivation.

Local-to-global methods for bounding the mixing times of Markov chains [KO20, AL20, GM20, CLV21, Ana+22] have enjoyed immense success in recent years in conjunction with the spectral independence framework of [ALG20, Che+21, Fen+22, Ana+22]. The basic idea intrinsic to these techniques is imposing on the state space a simplicial complex structure and analyzing the global chain by way of analyzing smaller local chains, which are easier for analysis. While the idea of decomposing the state space hierarchically and using intermediate chains to establish a log-Sobolev or Poincaré inequality is a classical idea in the study of Markov chains [Kai04, EF23, EF23b, Hei20, Che24, Jer+04, HS23, FM92], the ideas involved in the classical works are typically of a combinatorial nature. In contrast, the ideas employed by the local-to-global framework are often more analytical or algebraic.

In this work, we adapt the local-to-global machinery to a well-studied chain on triangulations of a convex polygon. This walk is one of the most well-known random walks on the so-called Catalan structures (see [Ald00, Ald03, Coh16, Ard03, Wil04, MRS97, MT97, EF23]). Catalan structures are a class of naturally defined combinatorial objects. These include but are not limited to Dyck paths (paths in a lattice that stay above a particular line); balanced sequences of ones and zeroes; non-crossing chord diagrams; integer partitions; binary plane trees; and triangulations of a convex polgyon. Chains on generalizations of Catalan structures have also been studied [EF23b, CS20, Ana+25].

A few of the Catalan structures (and their generalizations) are susceptible to recent methods using the theory of simplicial complexes (e.g. the Catalan matroid studied by [Ard03]). Others, such as the case of triangulations (and the isomorphic chain on binary search trees), have proven resistant to these methods.

In contrast, a few results over the past several years have achieved some success applying the classical method of canonical paths, namely in the cases of triangulations [EF23] and non-crossing spanning trees [Ana+25]. The canonical paths technique, along with its generalization to multicommodity flows, is useful in bounding conductance or, when the paths are not too long, in directly establishing a Poincaré inequality [DS91, Sin92].

The Aldous conjecture.

A famous conjecture of [Ald94] states that the relaxation time of the triangulation flip walk should be Θ⁡(n3/2)\Theta(n^{3/2}). [MRS97] proved that the mixing time is Ω⁡(n3/2)\Omega(n^{3/2}), but a matching upper bound still has not been found. [MT97] proved an O~​(n5)\widetilde{O}(n^{5}) upper bound11 1 where we recall that Ω~​(∙)\widetilde{\Omega}(\bullet) and O~​(∙)\widetilde{O}(\bullet) hide polylogarithmic factors in nn via a comparison argument, using a tight result by Wilson [Wil04] for the chain on Dyck paths. [EF23] proved an O~​(n3)\widetilde{O}(n^{3}) upper bound, the best known result until this paper.

Transport flows.

Recently [Che+25] proved a refinement of the mixing result of [JS89] for the natural random walk on perfect matchings using a technique they called transport flows. This technique morally combines the “best of both worlds” from simplicial local-to-global methods and canonical paths. That is, in the case of both the recent local-to-global methods and also older decomposition techniques, one generally must consider the spectral gap of each intermediate localized walk in the hierarchy, and one incurs a multiplicative loss in the spectral gap at each level of the decomposition. This may lead to an undesirable blow-up in the relaxation time (inverse spectral gap) unless the structures considered are all strong expanders. In such a setting, it would be more desirable to trade a multiplicative loss for an additive one.

While the result of [Che+25] trades the multiplicative loss for an additive one, using ideas similar to classical flow-based techniques, it is limited in the sense that the techniques only apply when the state space has a specific structure (a partite simplical complex). One of our main contributions will be extending these ideas to a more general decomposition framework, more in line with classical decomposition techniques, e.g. [Jer+04] etc.

Multi-way single-commodity flows.

Inspired by the results of [Che+25], we turn to a previous result proven in [EF23]. This result used a multicommodity flow (a well-studied generalization of canonical paths) with bounded congestion in the state space of the triangulation walk, replacing the multiplicative loss with an additive loss using a construction analogous to transport flows. However, this combinatorial bound proved a bound on the conductance and consequently suffered a quadratic loss in bounding the spectral gap, due to the celebrated Cheeger inequality, [AM85, Che15].

A natural way to bound the spectral gap, without the aforementioned quadratic loss, is to appeal to the local-to-global methods. However, as the structures considered do not appear to meet the very strong expansion required of these methods, this is unlikely to work.

Our contribution.

We generalize the transport flow technique of [Che+25] from the setting of partite complexes to a more general decomposition framework. Naïvely, a limitation of the flow-based techniques is the length of the paths used [DS91], and indeed this limitation also manifests in the techniques of [Che+25]. Inspired by [Mon14], we will avoid the quadratic loss and get a sharper spectral gap bound for the triangulation flip walk by studying the average congestion. These ideas will culminate in an O~​(n2)\widetilde{O}(n^{2}) relaxation time bound for the triangulation flip chain, which improves upon the relaxation time bound of O~​(n3)\widetilde{O}(n^{3}) proven in [EF23].

To obtain an O~​(n2)\widetilde{O}(n^{2}) mixing time bound, we will prove a log-Sobolev inequality for the triangulation flip chain. It is well known that a bound on the relaxation time can be converted to a bound on the mixing time, while suffering a logarithmic loss in the size of the state space [DS96]. Usually, and indeed in the case of triangulations, this factor is unfortunately linear in the problem size nn. Since our results are decomposition based, by appealing to this comparison when the compared chains are small enough, we only suffer a doubly logarithmic loss in the size of the state space, and consequently only a polylogarithmic loss in nn.

This O~​(n2)\widetilde{O}(n^{2}) mixing time bound on the triangulation flip chain improves the state of the art mixing time of O~​(n3)\widetilde{O}(n^{3}) by [EF23], while also getting an improved result for the spectral gap and a novel log-Sobolev inequality. Our technical contribution can be thought of as a more efficient way of leveraging transport flow constructions, which we hope will inspire further research in the future.

Our main results are as follows.

Theorem 1.1 (Functional Inequalities for the Flip Chain).

The triangulation walk satisfies a log-Sobolev inequality with constant Ω~​(n−2)\widetilde{\Omega}(n^{-2}), and has spectral gap Ω~​(n−2)\widetilde{\Omega}(n^{-2}).

Corollary 1.2 (Mixing Time for the Flip Walk).

The mixing time of the triangulation walk is O~​(n2)\widetilde{O}(n^{2}).

As mentioned before, our results avoid the Cheeger loss, by bounding the average congestion of the flow we analyze. This will follow by an analysis of the heights of binary trees and insights concerning the isomorphism between the triangulation walk and the natural rotation walk on binary trees (see e.g. [STT88, HP91, Coh16]).

Montenegro [Mon14] noted that the average vertex congestion is essentially equivalent to the expected path length in a multicommodity flow; so our result can be thought of as a dual version of [Che+25] utilizing the average congestion in place of the expected path length.

2 Preliminaries

2.1 Random Walks and Mixing Times

A random walk matrix P∈ℝΩ×ΩP\in\mathbb{R}^{\Omega\times\Omega} is a matrix with non-negative entries, all of whose rows sum to 1. Formally,

∀x,y∈Ω:P⁡(x,y)≥0and∀x∈Ω:∑y∈ΩP⁡(x,y)=1.\forall~x,y\in\Omega:~P(x,y)\geq 0\qquad\textrm{and}\qquad\forall~x\in\Omega:~\sum_{y\in\Omega}P(x,y)=1.

A distribution π:Ω→[0,1]\pi:\Omega\to[0,1] is called stationary for PP if, π​P=π\pi P=\pi. The walk described by PP is reversible, if the following detailed balance conditions hold:

π⁡(x)​P​(x,y)=π⁡(y)​P​(y,x),∀x,y∈Ω.\pi(x)P(x,y)=\pi(y)P(y,x)\,,\quad\quad\forall~x,y\in\Omega.

We will also write α⁡(P)=minx∈Ω⁡P⁡(x,x)\alpha(P)=\min_{x\in\Omega}P(x,x) for the holding probability of the random walk PP and π∗=minx∈Ω⁡π⁡(x)\pi^{*}~=~\min_{x\in\Omega}\pi(x) for the minimum measure of π\pi.

The ϵ\epsilon-mixing time of a random walk is defined to be the least time point such that after tt steps of random walk according to PP, the distribution of the random walk is ϵ\epsilon-close to the stationary distribution regardless of the initial distribution, i.e.

τ𝚖𝚒𝚡(P,ϵ)=min{t∈ℕ|‖π−μPt‖𝚃𝚅≤ϵ,for all probability distributionsμ:Ω→[0,1]},\tau_{\mathtt{mix}}(P,\epsilon)=\min\left\{t\in\mathbb{N}~\left|~\left\|\pi-\mu P^{t}\right\|_{\mathtt{TV}}\leq\epsilon\,,~\textrm{for all probability distributions}~\mu:\Omega\to[0,1]\right.\right\},

where ‖μ−ν‖𝚃𝚅=1/2⋅∑x∈Ω|μ⁡(x)−ν⁡(x)|\left\|\mu-\nu\right\|_{\mathtt{TV}}=1/2\cdot\sum_{x\in\Omega}|\mu(x)-\nu(x)|.

2.2 Projection-Restriction and Product Chains

Let (Ω,P,π)(\Omega,P,\pi) be an ergodic Markov chain and Ω=⋃t∈TΩt\Omega=\bigcup_{t\in T}\Omega_{t} a decomposition of its state space. When the stationary distribution π\pi is clear from context, we will simply write (Ω,P)(\Omega,P) in place of (Ω,P,π)(\Omega,P,\pi). We write π¯​(t)=π​(Ωt)\bar{\pi}(t)=\pi(\Omega_{t}) for all t∈Tt\in T and define the projection chain by the triple (Ω¯,P¯,π¯)(\overline{\Omega},\overline{P},\bar{\pi}) where

P¯​(t,t′)=∑x∈Ωt,y∈Ωt′π⁡(x)​P​(x,y)∑z∈Ωtπ⁡(z),\overline{P}(t,t^{\prime})=\frac{\sum_{x\in\Omega_{t},y\in\Omega_{t}^{\prime}}\pi(x)P(x,y)}{\sum_{z\in\Omega_{t}}\pi(z)}\,, (projection chain)

when t≠t′t\neq t^{\prime} and with self loops for the remaining probabilities. That is, the probability of transitioning from class tt to t′t^{\prime} in the projection chain is the probability we transition from any element of Ωt\Omega_{t} to any element of Ωt′\Omega_{t^{\prime}} in the original chain conditioned on being in Ωt\Omega_{t}. Naturally, by defining πt​(x)=π⁡(x)π⁡(Ωt)\pi_{t}(x)=\frac{\pi(x)}{\pi(\Omega_{t})} we can also define the restriction chain as the triple (Ωt,Pt,πt)(\Omega_{t},P_{t},\pi_{t}) where

Pt​(x,y)=P⁡(x,y)∑z∈ΩtP⁡(x,z),P_{t}(x,y)=\frac{P(x,y)}{\sum_{z\in\Omega_{t}}P(x,z)}\,, (restriction chain)

for all x,y∈Ωtx,y\in\Omega_{t}.

Let kk be a positive integer, (Ω,Pi,πi), 1≤i≤k(\Omega_{,}P_{i},\pi_{i}),\ 1\leq i\leq k be Markov chains and ww a distribution on kk. Consider the product chain (Ω,P,π)(\Omega,P,\pi) with Ω=∏i=1nΩi\Omega=\prod_{i=1}^{n}\Omega_{i} and

P(x,y)=∑i=1nwiPi(xi,yi)∏j≠i𝟙{xj=yj}.P(x,y)=\sum_{i=1}^{n}w_{i}P_{i}(x_{i},y_{i})\prod_{j\neq i}\mathbbm{1}\{x_{j}=y_{j}\}. (product chain)

Equivalently, the transition from every state consists of picking a coordinate in [k][k] according to ww and then change this coordinate according to (Ωi,Pi)(\Omega_{i},P_{i}). It is straightforward to verify that the stationary distribution of the product chain is π=⨂i=1nπi\pi=\bigotimes_{i=1}^{n}\pi_{i}. We note that the graph which underlies the product chain corresponds to a weighted Cartesian product of the graphs which underlie the individual chains (Ω,Pi,πi)(\Omega,P_{i},\pi_{i}).

Varπ⁡(f)=𝔼π​[f2]−(𝔼π​f)2=⟨f,(I−Jπ)​f⟩π.\operatorname{Var}_{\pi}(f)=\mathbb{E}_{\pi}[f^{2}]-\left\lparen\mathbb{E}_{\pi}f\right\rparen^{2}=\left\langle f,(I-J_{\pi})f\right\rangle_{\pi}. (variance)

If ⋃t∈TΩt\bigcup_{t\in T}\Omega_{t} is a decomposition of Ω\Omega, then the following equation is known as the law of total variance

Varπ⁡(f)=Varπ¯⁡F+𝔼t∼π¯​Varπt​f,\operatorname{Var}_{\pi}(f)=\operatorname{Var}_{\overline{\pi}}F+\mathbb{E}_{t\sim\overline{\pi}}\operatorname{Var}_{\pi_{t}}f, (law of total variance)

The second functional we will need is that of entropy. If f:Ω→ℝ≥0f:\Omega\to\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0} is a non-negative function, the entropy Entπ⁡(f)\operatorname{Ent}_{\pi}(f) of ff is

2.4 Catalan Structures: Triangulations and Trees

A triangulation of a point set (in, say, the Euclidean plane) is a maximal collection of pairwise non-crossing edges connecting pairs of points. In the special case that the point set is convex, every triangulation of the point set includes the convex hull, and thus we will assume the point set is a convex polygon. Since the edges belonging to the convex hull are in every triangulation, we will identify a triangulation xx by its set of non-hull edges, and we will call these edges diagonals.

Given a diagonal dd, it will be convenient for us to define the length of dd to be the number of edges in a shortest path consisting of polygon edges that connects the two endpoints of dd.

One can view a triangulation naturally as a planar graph. The dual graph of a convex polygon triangulation is a binary tree. One can orient the polygon so that the dual tree is rooted, and therefore the number of triangulations of an n+2n+2-gon is equal to the number of binary plane trees with nn nodes. This is known to be equal to the Catalan number [HP91]

Cn=1n+1​(2​nn).C_{n}=\frac{1}{n+1}\binom{2n}{n}\,.

Notice that the Catalan numbers satisfy the recurrence relation,

Cn=∑j=1nCj−1​Cn−j,C_{n}=\sum_{j=1}^{n}C_{j-1}C_{n-j}\,,

where C0=1C_{0}=1 (see for example, [GKP94, Chapters 5 and 7]). With this, it is easy to observe that CnC_{n} counts the number of rooted subtrees of the infinite binary tree on nn vertices, or equivalently, unlabelled rooted plane trees on nn-vertices. Henceforth, we will refer to such trees as Catalan trees.

Using Stirling’s formula, CnC_{n} is seen to grow asymptotically as Θ⁡(1n3/2⋅4n)\Theta\left(\frac{1}{n^{3/2}}\cdot 4^{n}\right).

The triangulation flip walk (which we will also call the triangulation walk) is the following random walk, defined with respect to the regular n+2n+2-gon: start with an arbitrary triangulation xx. Then repeatedly flip a uniformly random diagonal dd of the current triangulation: that is, remove dd and replace it with the unique diagonal d′≠dd^{\prime}\neq d that can be added to the triangulation xx without introducing a crossing. (The removal of dd induces a quadrilateral formed by the two triangles incident to dd. The existence and uniqueness of d′d^{\prime} can be seen to follow from the convexity of the n+2n+2-gon.) We impose a holding probability of 1/2 (see Section 2.1).

The flip walk is invariant to perturbations of the n+2n+2-gon, so long as it remains convex.

The flip walk is known to be isomorphic to the rotation walk (see e.g. [STT88]) on binary trees. A rotation in a binary tree is an operation of one of two forms. The first form is as follows: take a parent node zz and a left child ww of zz. Replace zz by ww: that is, make ww a child of the parent of zz (a left child if zz is a left child, a right child if zz is a right child)—or, if zz is the root, make ww the root. Let ww retain its left child; let zz retain its right child. Then, let uu be the right child of ww; and make uu the new left child of zz.

The second form is the mirror image of the first: let ww be a right child of zz, and proceed as in the first case but with left and right reversed.

The rotation walk is as follows: start with an arbitrary binary tree on nn nodes. Then repeatedly choose a uniformly random edge in the current tree, and perform a rotation at the parent node of that edge. (Impose a 1/21/2 holding probability as in the triangulation walk.)

The isomorphism between the two walks follows from observing the correspondence between a triangulation flip and a tree rotation.

2.5 Multicommodity Flows and Canonical paths

A standard technique in bounding the mixing times of Markov chains uses canonical paths. The idea is to show that the state space of the chain is in some sense free of “bottlenecks,” by finding a path between each pair of states such that no edge belongs to too many paths. A generalization of canonical paths is to construct a multicommodity flow: a collection of flow functions in which for every pair of states s,t∈Ωs,t\in\Omega, ss sends a unit of flow to tt through paths in the state space Ω\Omega. The congestion of a multicommodity flow is the maximum, over all edges, of the amount of flow sent across the edge, summed over all s,ts,t pairs that use the edge.

Two classical theorems relate canonical paths (more generally, multicommodity flows) to mixing. The first uses the Cheeger inequalities to obtain an upper bound on the relaxation time from an upper bound on the congestion in a multicommodity flow. However, one suffers a quadratic cost in this process, as well as an additional cost in passing from the relaxation time to the mixing time, [Tre13, Theorem 2.1]. The latter problem can be solved in some cases using a result in [LK99]. [EF23] used this theorem to obtain an O~​(n3)\widetilde{O}(n^{3}) mixing time for the triangulation walk.

Another theorem [DS91] allows one to pass from flows to relaxation time without the quadratic cost; however, one trades this cost for a cost incurred in analyzing the worst-case length of a path in the construction. The worst-case path length is sufficiently long in the construction in [EF23] that it is not clear how to apply the theorem in this case.

In this paper, rather than using multicommodity flows, it will be useful to consider a flow function from one set of states S⊆ΩS\subseteq\Omega to a set T⊆ΩT\subseteq\Omega, where we only use a single commodity. [EF23] gave a notion of multi-way single commodity flows. We adapt the formulation as follows.

Given S,T⊆ΩS,T\subseteq\Omega where S∩T=∅S\cap T=\emptyset, let an SS-TT flow be a function ϕ:{(x,y)∈Ω2∣P⁡(x,y)>0}→ℝ\phi:\{(x,y)\in\Omega^{2}\mid P(x,y)>0\}\rightarrow\mathbb{R} such that ϕ⁡(x,y)=−ϕ⁡(y,x)\phi(x,y)=-\phi(y,x) for all x,yx,y, and such that, defining the net flow out of a state x∈Ωx\in\Omega to be ∑y∈Ω:P⁡(x,y)>0ϕ(x,y)\sum_{y\in\Omega:P(x,y)>0}\phi(x,y):

  1. 1.

    the net flow out of each x∈Sx\in S is equal to π⁡(T)\pi(T) ,

  2. 2.

    the net flow into each y∈Ty\in T is equal to π⁡(S)\pi(S) , and

  3. 3.

    the net flow into (and the net flow out of) each x∈Ω∖(S∪T)x\in\Omega\setminus\left(S\cup T\right) is zero.

(Here, if the net flow out of xx is ϕ\phi then we let the net flow into xx be −ϕ-\phi.)

3 Transport Flows

We recall the definition of transport flows from [Che+25]. Let (Ω,P,π)(\Omega,P,\pi) be an ergodic Markov chain and μ,ν\mu,\nu distributions supported on Ω\Omega. A transport flow from μ\mu to ν\nu is a distribution Γ\Gamma of paths such that when γ\gamma is drawn from Γ\Gamma, the starting state of the path is distributed according to μ\mu and the ending state according to ν\nu. We will denote the starting and ending states of the path γ\gamma by s⁡(γ)s(\gamma) and t⁡(γ)t(\gamma) respectively.

We will assume for convenience that for every x,y∈Ωx,y\in\Omega with P⁡(x,y)>0P(x,y)>0 the transitions (x,y)(x,y) and (y,x)(y,x) are not both used in the construction: i.e. for every γ\gamma such that Γ⁡(γ)>0\Gamma(\gamma)>0, if (x,y)∈γ(x,y)\in\gamma then for all γ′\gamma^{\prime} such that Γ⁡(γ′)>0\Gamma(\gamma^{\prime})>0 we have (y,x)∉γ′(y,x)\notin\gamma^{\prime}.

It is easy to modify any transport flow to satisfy this condition (Lemma A.1).

Let S,T⊆ΩS,T\subseteq\Omega. A transport flow from SS to TT is a transport flow from μ=πS\mu=\pi_{S} to ν=πT\nu=\pi_{T}, where πS\pi_{S} is supported on SS, πT\pi_{T} is supported on TT, and μ⁡(x)=πS​(x)=π⁡(x)π⁡(S)\mu(x)=\pi_{S}(x)=\frac{\pi(x)}{\pi(S)} for all x∈Sx\in S, and similarly ν​(x)=πT​(x)\nu(x)=\pi_{T}(x) for all x∈Tx\in T.

Let f:Ω→ℝf:\Omega\rightarrow\mathbb{R} be an arbitrary function. Let F⁡(S)=𝔼x∼πS​f​(x)F(S)=\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\pi_{S}}f(x) be the expectation of ff over πS\pi_{S}.

The main tool we will use for establishing our functional inequalities will be the following result,

Theorem 3.1.

Let S,T⊆ΩS,T\subseteq\Omega. Suppose a transport flow Γ\Gamma exists from SS to TT where the maximum congestion is ρ\rho, i.e. for all x,y∈Ωx,y\in\Omega,

ϕx​y:=π⁡(S)​π​(T)π⁡(x)​P​(x,y)⋅𝔼γ∼Γ[1[(x,y)∈γ]]≤ρ.\phi_{xy}:=\frac{\pi(S)\pi(T)}{\pi(x)P(x,y)}\cdot\mathbb{E}_{\gamma\sim\Gamma}\left[1[(x,y)\in\gamma]\right]\leq\rho\,.

The average congestion is

ρ¯=∑x,y∈Ωϕx​yπ(x)P(x,y)=π(S)π(T)∑x,y∈Ω𝔼γ∼Γ1[(x,y)∈γ].\bar{\rho}=\sum_{x,y\in\Omega}\phi_{xy}\pi(x)P(x,y)=\pi(S)\pi(T)\sum_{x,y\in\Omega}\mathbb{E}_{\gamma\sim\Gamma}1[(x,y)\in\gamma]\,.

Then

π⁡(S)​π​(T)​(F⁡(S)−F⁡(T))2≤ρ¯​ρπ⁡(S)​π​(T)​∑x,y∈Ωπ⁡(x)​P​(x,y)​(f⁡(x)−f⁡(y))2.\pi(S)\pi(T)(F(S)-F(T))^{2}\leq\frac{\bar{\rho}\rho}{\pi(S)\pi(T)}\sum_{x,y\in\Omega}\pi(x)P(x,y)(f(x)-f(y))^{2}\,. (3.1)

A precursor of Theorem 3.1 using average path length instead of average congestion already appeared in [Che+25]. For concreteness, we present an equivalent formulation of their result below,

Theorem 3.2 (Theorem 10, [Che+25]).

Let S,T⊆ΩS,T\subseteq\Omega. Suppose a transport flow Γ\Gamma from SS to TT exists, where for every x,y∈Ωx,y\in\Omega satisfying y∼xy\sim x, we have

π⁡(S)​π​(T)π⁡(x)​P​(x,y)⋅𝔼γ∼Γ​[1[(x,y)∈γ]|γ|]≤κ\frac{\pi(S)\pi(T)}{\pi(x)P(x,y)}\cdot\mathbb{E}_{\gamma\sim\Gamma}\left[\frac{1[(x,y)\in\gamma]}{|\gamma|}\right]\leq\kappa

and 𝔼γ∼Γ​[|γ|2]≤L\mathbb{E}_{\gamma\sim\Gamma}\left[|\gamma|^{2}\right]\leq L.

Then for any function f:Ω→ℝf:\Omega\rightarrow\mathbb{R}

π⁡(S)​π​(T)​(F⁡(S)−F⁡(T))2≤κ​L​∑x,y∈Ωπ⁡(x)​P​(x,y)​(f⁡(x)−f⁡(y))2.\pi(S)\pi(T)(F(S)-F(T))^{2}\leq\kappa L\sum_{x,y\in\Omega}\pi(x)P(x,y)(f(x)-f(y))^{2}\,.

We now present the proof of Theorem 3.1.

Proof of Theorem 3.1.

Let ϕx​y=∑γΓ⁡(γ)​π⁡(S)​π​(T)π⁡(x)​P​(x,y)\phi_{xy}=\sum_{\gamma}\Gamma(\gamma)\frac{\pi(S)\pi(T)}{\pi(x)P(x,y)}. We have

=∑(x,y)∑γ:(x,y)∈γΓ(γ)π(S)π(T)|f(x)−f(y)|\displaystyle=\sum_{(x,y)}\sum_{\gamma:(x,y)\in\gamma}\Gamma(\gamma)\pi(S)\pi(T)|f(x)-f(y)|
=∑(x,y)ϕx​y​π​(x)​P​(x,y)​|f⁡(x)−f⁡(y)|.\displaystyle=\sum_{(x,y)}\phi_{xy}\pi(x)P(x,y)|f(x)-f(y)|\,. (3.2)

Therefore

(π⁡(S)​π​(T)​(F⁡(S)−F⁡(T)))2\displaystyle\left(\pi(S)\pi(T)(F(S)-F(T))\right)^{2} ≤(∑(x,y)∈Ωϕx​y​π​(x)​P​(x,y)​|f⁡(x)−f⁡(y)|)2\displaystyle\leq\Bigl(\sum_{(x,y)\in\Omega}\phi_{xy}\pi(x)P(x,y)|f(x)-f(y)|\Bigr)^{2}
≤(∑(x,y)∈Ωϕx​y​π​(x)​P​(x,y))\displaystyle\leq\Bigl(\sum_{(x,y)\in\Omega}\phi_{xy}\pi(x)P(x,y)\Bigr) (3.3)
⋅(∑(x,y)∈Ωϕx​y​π​(x)​P​(x,y)​(f⁡(x)−f⁡(y))2),\displaystyle\quad\cdot\Bigl(\sum_{(x,y)\in\Omega}\phi_{xy}\pi(x)P(x,y)(f(x)-f(y))^{2}\Bigr)\,, (3.4)

by the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality. (3.3) is ρ¯\bar{\rho}; the claim follows. ∎

In [Mon14] it was observed that average path length and average congestion are highly related parameters; for our proofs it will be more convenient to work with the latter parameter. Indeed, our proof of Theorem 3.1 is inspired by the proof of Theorem 3.2 in [Che+25].

The utility of Theorem 3.1 is that it provides a way to bypass the Cheeger inequality when one has paths that can be long in the worst case but where the average congestion is small. (This is true for the construction of [EF23].) It is important to find sufficiently large sets S,TS,T between which to send the flow, however, as the denominator of the right-hand side of (3.1) indicates.

It will be useful for our purposes to refine Theorem 3.1 as follows:

Corollary 3.3.

Let S,T⊆ΩS,T\subseteq\Omega. Suppose a transport flow Γ\Gamma exists from SS to TT where the maximum congestion is ρ\rho and the paths in the flow only use edges between vertices in S∪TS\cup T.

Let

ρ¯S=π(T)∑x∈S,y∈S∪T𝔼γ∼Γ1[(x,y)∈γ]\bar{\rho}_{S}=\pi(T)\sum_{x\in S,y\in S\cup T}\mathbb{E}_{\gamma\sim\Gamma}1[(x,y)\in\gamma]

be the average congestion across edges having an endpoint in SS, and define ρ¯T\bar{\rho}_{T} symmetrically.

Then

π⁡(S)​π​(T)​(F⁡(S)−F⁡(T))2\displaystyle\pi(S)\pi(T)(F(S)-F(T))^{2} ≤ρ​ρ¯Sπ⁡(T)​∑x∈S,y∈S∪Tπ⁡(x)​P​(x,y)​(f⁡(x)−f⁡(y))2\displaystyle\leq\frac{\rho\bar{\rho}_{S}}{\pi(T)}\sum_{x\in S,y\in S\cup T}\pi(x)P(x,y)(f(x)-f(y))^{2}
+ρ​ρ¯Tπ⁡(S)∑x∈T,y∈S∪Tπ(x)P(x,y)(f(x)−f(y))2.\displaystyle\quad\quad+\frac{\rho\bar{\rho}_{T}}{\pi(S)}\sum_{x\in T,y\in S\cup T}\pi(x)P(x,y)(f(x)-f(y))^{2}\,. (3.5)
Proof.

The theorem follows from the proof of Theorem 3.1 and the observation that, by the definition of ρ¯\bar{\rho}, we have ρ¯=π⁡(S)​ρ¯S+π⁡(T)​ρ¯T\bar{\rho}=\pi(S)\bar{\rho}_{S}+\pi(T)\bar{\rho}_{T}. ∎

The following will allow us to pass from a combinatorial flow construction to a transport flow:

Lemma 3.4.

Given (Ω,P,π)(\Omega,P,\pi), let S,T⊆ΩS,T\subseteq\Omega. Let ϕ\phi be an SS-TT flow. Then there exists a transport flow ΓS→T\Gamma^{S\rightarrow T} satisfying, for each edge (x,y)(x,y) such that ϕ⁡(x,y)≥0\phi(x,y)\geq 0:

∑γ∋(x,y)Γ⁡(γ)=ϕ⁡(x,y).\sum_{\gamma\ni(x,y)}\Gamma(\gamma)=\phi(x,y)\,.

The proof of Lemma 3.4 uses a straightforward iterative process of increasing the flow across a path until an edge becomes “tight”; the argument is straightforward but we defer the details to Appendix A.

4 O~​(n2)\widetilde{O}(n^{2}) Mixing for Triangulations

4.1 Decomposing the Triangulation Walk and Outline of the Proof

We begin by presenting the two key partitions of the triangulation state space given by [MRS97] and [EF23] and outlining some of their main properties. The central triangle of a triangulation is the triangle which contains the center of the polygon; in the case where the center lies on one of the diagonals, we slightly perturb the center so that it lies in a unique triangle.

Let TT be the set of central triangles. Define the central triangle partition as the projection chain (Ω¯=T,P¯,π¯)\left(\overline{\Omega}=T,\overline{P},\overline{\pi}\right) corresponding to the decomposition Ωt={x∈Ω∣x​ includes the central triangle ​t}\Omega_{t}=\{x\in\Omega\mid x\textnormal{ includes the central triangle }t\}. Recall that the transitions are given by

P¯​(t,t′)=∑x∈Ωt,y∈Ωt′π⁡(x)​P​(x,y)∑z∈Ωtπ⁡(z),\overline{P}(t,t^{\prime})=\frac{\sum_{x\in\Omega_{t},y\in\Omega_{t^{\prime}}}\pi(x)P(x,y)}{\sum_{z\in\Omega_{t}}\pi(z)}\,,

when t≠t′t\neq t^{\prime} and with self loops for the remaining probabilities, while the stationary distribution π¯\overline{\pi} satisfies π¯​(t)=π⁡(Ωt)=∑x∈Ωtπ⁡(x)\overline{\pi}(t)=\pi(\Omega_{t})=\sum_{x\in\Omega_{t}}\pi(x). According to the law of total variance, we may decompose

Varπ⁡f=Varπ¯⁡F+𝔼t∼π¯​Varπt​f.\operatorname{Var}_{\pi}f=\operatorname{Var}_{\overline{\pi}}F+\mathbb{E}_{t\sim\overline{\pi}}\operatorname{Var}_{\pi_{t}}f.

Since our goal is to obtain a Poincaré inequality, we want to bound both the terms by the Dirichlet form of the overall chain. Note that the second term is the average restricted variance in Ωt\Omega_{t}, i.e. over triangulations with a given central triangle tt. As the average of the Dirichlet forms of the restrictions is bounded by Dirichlet form of the overall chain (this is straightforward to check, but we will prove it explicitly when we use it), we need a meaningful Poincaré inequality for each restriction chain. A crucial observation is that every restriction chain is in fact a product chain over smaller triangulation walks (see Figure 1). This, combined with Lemma 2.5, will enable us to obtain a recursive bound on the Poincaré constant.

Lemma 4.1 ([EF23]).

For each state t∈Ω¯t\in\overline{\Omega}, the restriction chain (Ωt,Pt,πt)(\Omega_{t},P_{t},\pi_{t}) is the Cartesian product of three chains (Ωt(1),Pt(1),πt(1)),(Ωt(2),Pt(2),πt(2)),(Ωt(3),Pt(3),πt(3))(\Omega_{t}^{(1)},P_{t}^{(1)},\pi_{t}^{(1)}),(\Omega_{t}^{(2)},P_{t}^{(2)},\pi_{t}^{(2)}),(\Omega_{t}^{(3)},P_{t}^{(3)},\pi_{t}^{(3)}) each of which is isomorphic to the triangulation walk on a smaller polygon (possibly empty) on at most n/2+1n/2+1 vertices.

Remark 4.2.

The last part of the lemma is crucial for our recursive argument. As each iteration reduces the problem to polygons of at most half the size of the original, we perform only a logarithmic number of iterations.

It remains to bound Varπ¯⁡F\operatorname{Var}_{\overline{\pi}}F, the variance on the projection chain, by the Dirichlet form on the overall chain. This will be done using the transport flow machinery from Section 3. The flow construction naturally points to studying boundaries between Ωt,Ωt′\Omega_{t},\Omega_{t^{\prime}} for different central triangles, in which a new projection chain will arise.

Define the oriented partition chain as the projection chain (Ω^=[n],P^,π^)\left(\hat{\Omega}=[n],\hat{P},\hat{\pi}\right) corresponding to the decomposition Ωi={x∈Ω∣x​ includes the triangle ​(0,i,n+1)}\Omega_{i}=\{x\in\Omega\mid x\textnormal{ includes the triangle }(0,i,n+1)\}, with P^,π^\hat{P},\hat{\pi} defined in an analogous fashion to P¯,π¯\overline{P},\overline{\pi}. Given S⊆Ω^S\subseteq\hat{\Omega}, we will write Ω⁡[S]:=⋃i∈SΩi\Omega[S]:=\bigcup_{i\in S}\Omega_{i}.

Given t,t′∈Ω¯t,t^{\prime}\in\overline{\Omega} with P¯​(t,t′)>0\overline{P}(t,t^{\prime})>0, define

Ωt​t′={x∈Ωt∣∃y∈Ωt′,P(x,y)>0}.\Omega_{tt^{\prime}}=\left\{x\in\Omega_{t}\mid\exists y\in\Omega_{t^{\prime}},P(x,y)>0\right\}\,.

The set Ωt​t′\Omega_{tt^{\prime}} is the set of states in Ωt\Omega_{t} having a neighboring state in Ωt′\Omega_{t^{\prime}}.

Similarly given i,j∈Ω^i,j\in\hat{\Omega} (recall that for all i,ji,j, P^​(i,j)>0\hat{P}(i,j)>0), define

Ωi​j={x∈Ωi∣∃y∈Ωj,P(i,j)>0}.\Omega_{ij}=\left\{x\in\Omega_{i}\mid\exists y\in\Omega_{j},P(i,j)>0\right\}\,.

See Fig. 2.

The central triangle tt partitions the polygon into three smaller polygons (one of which may be the empty polgyon). Label the sub-polygon containing the triangle uu as polygon (1); label the other two sub-polgyons as (2) and (3). Consider any partial triangulation in which sub-polygons (2) and (3) are fully triangulated, but sub-polygon (1) is not triangulated. Denote such a sub-triangulation as η∈Ωt(2)×Ωt(3)\eta\in\Omega_{t}^{(2)}\times\Omega_{t}^{(3)}. Given η\eta, let Ω(t,η)\Omega^{(t,\eta)} denote the set of states in Ωt\Omega_{t} having sub-polygons (2) and (3) triangulated according to η\eta.

We extend this notation and use (Ω(t,η),P(t,η),π(t,η))\left(\Omega^{(t,\eta)},P^{(t,\eta)},\pi^{(t,\eta)}\right) to refer respectively to the copy of the chain (Ωt(1),Pt(1),πt(1))\left(\Omega_{t}^{(1)},P_{t}^{(1)},\pi_{t}^{(1)}\right) induced by fixing η\eta. Given a function f:Ω→ℝf:\Omega\rightarrow\mathbb{R} and given t∈Ω¯t\in\overline{\Omega} and given η∈Ωt(2)×Ωt(3)\eta\in\Omega_{t}^{(2)}\times\Omega_{t}^{(3)}, define the function f(t,η):Ω(t,η)→ℝf^{(t,\eta)}:\Omega^{(t,\eta)}\rightarrow\mathbb{R} so that, if z∈Ω(t,η)z\in\Omega^{(t,\eta)} we let f(t,η)​(z)=f⁡(z∪η)f^{(t,\eta)}(z)=f(z\cup\eta).

We will also denote by Δ\Delta the degree of the (regular) graph induced by the chain (Ω,P,π)(\Omega,P,\pi), and note that for all x,y∈Ωx,y\in\Omega such that P⁡(x,y)>0P(x,y)>0 we have P⁡(x,y)=1ΔP(x,y)=\frac{1}{\Delta}. (We have Δ=Θ⁡(n)\Delta=\Theta(n), but it will be useful for clarity to distinguish it as a variable.) We will denote by Δt(1)\Delta_{t}^{(1)} the degree of the graph induced by (Ωt(1),Pt(1),πt(1))\left(\Omega_{t}^{(1)},P_{t}^{(1)},\pi_{t}^{(1)}\right) and define Δt(2),Δt(3)\Delta_{t}^{(2)},\Delta_{t}^{(3)} similarly.

[EF23] observed that given t,t′∈Ω¯t,t^{\prime}\in\overline{\Omega}, the boundary set Ωt​t′\Omega_{tt^{\prime}} is precisely the set of triangulations that contain both the triangle tt, and a particular triangle uu formed by two vertices of tt and an additional vertex of t′t^{\prime}. Letting ii be that additional vertex of t′t^{\prime}, uu is the unique triangle having vertex ii and sharing its other two vertices with tt. See Figure 3.

We will denote by Ω^(t,η)\hat{\Omega}^{(t,\eta)} the set of all vertices ii induced by some triangle uu as described above, and denote by (Ω^(t,η),P^(t,η),π^(t,η))\left(\hat{\Omega}^{(t,\eta)},\hat{P}^{(t,\eta)},\hat{\pi}^{(t,\eta)}\right) the oriented projection chain induced by fixing the “special edge” to be the edge of uu that bounds polygon (1) (i.e., the edge (j,b)(j,b) in Figure 3). We then define F(t,η):Ω^(t,η)→ℝF^{(t,\eta)}:\hat{\Omega}^{(t,\eta)}\rightarrow\mathbb{R} so that

F(t,η)​(i):=∑z∈Ωi(t,η)π(t,η)​(z)π^(t,η)​(i).F^{(t,\eta)}(i):=\sum_{z\in\Omega_{i}^{(t,\eta)}}\frac{\pi^{(t,\eta)}(z)}{\hat{\pi}^{(t,\eta)}(i)}\,.

We have:

Lemma 4.3 ([EF23]).

For all t,t′∈Ω¯t,t^{\prime}\in\overline{\Omega} where P⁡(t,t′)>0P(t,t^{\prime})>0, for all η∈Ωt(2)×Ωt(3)\eta\in\Omega_{t}^{(2)}\times\Omega_{t}^{(3)}:

Ωt​t′=⋃η∈Ωt(2)×Ωt(3)Ωi(t,η),\Omega_{tt^{\prime}}=\bigcup_{\eta\in\Omega_{t}^{(2)}\times\Omega_{t}^{(3)}}\Omega_{i}^{(t,\eta)}\ \,, (4.1)

where by Ωi(t,η)⊆Ω(t,η)\Omega_{i}^{(t,\eta)}\subseteq\Omega^{(t,\eta)} we denote the set of states in Ω(t,η)\Omega^{(t,\eta)} that contain the triangle uu (having vertex ii) described above.

In other words, Eq. 4.1 states that a triangulation x∈Ωtx\in\Omega_{t} is in Ωt​t′\Omega_{tt^{\prime}} if and only if xx contains the triangle uu (which has vertex ii). These triangulations can then grouped according to how they triangulate Ωt(2)\Omega_{t}^{(2)} and Ωt(3)\Omega_{t}^{(3)}, and by definition this union is disjoint. See Figure 3.

Eq. 4.1 is a key observation that relates the central-triangle projection chain and the oriented projection chain. It allowed [EF23] to reduce the problem of sending flow between central-triangle projection states tt and t′t^{\prime} to two problems: (i) sending flow from the boundary set Ωt′​t\Omega_{t^{\prime}t} to Ωt​t′\Omega_{tt^{\prime}}, and (ii) sending flow from the boundary set Ωt​t′\Omega_{tt^{\prime}} to the rest of Ωt\Omega_{t}. Problem (i) is easy to solve as there is a perfect matching (see Lemma 4.6) between Ωt​t′\Omega_{tt^{\prime}} and Ωt′​t\Omega_{t^{\prime}t}. Problem (ii) was solved by reducing to the problem of sending flow from Ωi(t,η)\Omega_{i}^{(t,\eta)} to the rest of Ω(t,η)\Omega^{(t,\eta)}—that is, the problem of sending flow from a state in the oriented projection chain Ω^(t,η)\hat{\Omega}^{(t,\eta)} to the other states in that projection chain. This problem in turn, [EF23] showed (we will retrace the proof rigorously), can be recursively decomposed with no blowup in congestion.

4.2 Bounding the Variance of the Function over the Projection Chain

The aim of this section is to show the following lemma:

Lemma 4.4.

The variance of the function FF over the projection chain satisfies the inequality

Varπ¯⁡F≤C⁡(logc⁡n)​n2​ℰπ​(f),\operatorname{Var}_{\overline{\pi}}F\leq C(\log^{c}n)n^{2}\mathcal{E}_{\pi}(f)\,,

for all f:Ω→ℝf:\Omega\to\mathbb{R}, for some universal constants C,c>0C,c>0.

Lemma 4.4, combined with a hierarchical decomposition of the (variance of the) overall chain using the projection chain (Ω¯,P¯,π¯)(\overline{\Omega},\overline{P},\overline{\pi}), will allow us to establish the desired lower bound on the spectral gap.

[EF23] constructed a multicommodity flow in the projection chain (Ω¯,P¯,π¯)(\overline{\Omega},\overline{P},\overline{\pi}) and analyzed its congestion. Their analysis can be used to show the following (we show this in Appendix A):

for constants C1,c1>0C_{1},c_{1}>0, where νi,j\nu_{i,j} is the uniform distribution on Ωt(i)×Ωt(j)\Omega_{t}^{(i)}\times\Omega_{t}^{(j)}, and for all t,i,kt,i,k, S^k(t,η)⊆Ω^(t,η)\hat{S}_{k}^{(t,\eta)}\subseteq\hat{\Omega}^{(t,\eta)}, and Sk(t,η)=⋃i∈S^k(t,η)Ωi(t,η)S_{k}^{(t,\eta)}=\bigcup_{i\in\hat{S}_{k}^{(t,\eta)}}\Omega_{i}^{(t,\eta)}, and where π^​(S^k(t,η))≤3/4\hat{\pi}(\hat{S}_{k}^{(t,\eta)})\leq 3/4.

The term in the RHS of (4.2) describes the problem of sending flow between the boundary sets Ωt​t′\Omega_{tt^{\prime}} and Ωt′​t\Omega_{t^{\prime}t}; similarly the RHS of (4.3) describes the problem of sending flow from a set Sk(t,η)⊆Ω(t,η)S_{k}^{(t,\eta)}\subseteq\Omega^{(t,\eta)}, i.e. a union of subsets of the chain Ω(t,η)\Omega^{(t,\eta)}, to the rest of Ω(t,η)\Omega^{(t,\eta)}. The expectation runs over all partial triangulations in Ωt\Omega_{t} in which two of the three sub-polgyons are triangulated.

We derive Lemma 4.5 from [EF23a, Lemma 32], which is the congestion analysis of a flow construction. In the construction, each Ωt\Omega_{t} begins with uniformly concentrated flow that Ωt\Omega_{t} needs to route to the rest of Ω\Omega (through edges in Ω\Omega). (This flow problem corresponds to the terms of the form π¯​(t)​(F⁡(t)−𝔼π​f)2\overline{\pi}(t)(F(t)-\mathbb{E}_{\pi}f)^{2} in the variance of the projection function FF.) The authors then reduce the problem to a collection of flow subproblems in which (i) a pair of adjacent projection chain states send flow across the boundary between them, and (ii) a state tt receives flow from other states that it must distribute from its boundary throughout Ωt\Omega_{t}.

Subproblems of the form (i) correspond to (4.2), and subproblems of the form (ii) correspond to (4.3). For reasons specific to the flow construction, each subproblem of form (ii) involves distributing flow from multiple boundary sets (i.e. multiple states in the oriented projection chain Ω^(t,η)\hat{\Omega}^{(t,\eta)}), of the form S^k(t,η)⊆Ω^(t,η)\hat{S}_{k}^{(t,\eta)}\subseteq\hat{\Omega}^{(t,\eta)}.

The following insight from [EF23] will allow us to bound (4.2):

Lemma 4.6 (Lemma 8, [EF23]).

For all t,t′∈Ω¯t,t^{\prime}\in\overline{\Omega} such that P⁡(t,t′)>0P(t,t^{\prime})>0, the set of edges between states in Ωt​t′\Omega_{tt^{\prime}} and Ωt′​t\Omega_{t^{\prime}t} is a perfect matching.

Using Lemma 4.6 and the fact that π\pi is uniform, we prove (see e.g. [FM92, Jer+04] for a similar technique):

≤∑x∈Ωt​t′,y∈Ωt′​t:P⁡(x,y)>0π(x)P(x,y)(f(x)−f(y))2,\displaystyle\leq\sum_{x\in\Omega_{tt^{\prime}},y\in\Omega_{t^{\prime}t}:P(x,y)>0}\pi(x)P(x,y)\left(f(x)-f(y)\right)^{2}\,, (4.8)

4.3 Proof of the Main Theorem

The following is an immediate consequence of Lemma 2.1,

Lemma 4.10.

Let g:=f2g:=f^{2} (pointwise) and let G⁡(t):=𝔼x∼πt​g​(x)G(t):=\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\pi_{t}}g(x). Then

Varπ¯⁡G≤Varπ¯⁡F+𝔼t∼π¯​Varπt​f=Varπ⁡f.\operatorname{Var}_{\bar{\pi}}\sqrt{G}\leq\operatorname{Var}_{\bar{\pi}}F+\mathbb{E}_{t\sim\bar{\pi}}\operatorname{Var}_{\pi_{t}}f=\operatorname{Var}_{\pi}f\,.
Proof of Theorem 1.1.

We first prove the Poincaré inequality. We will use the law of total variance and the decomposition properties of the chain to get a recursive bound on the relaxation time. Let tnt_{n} be the relaxation time for the flip walk on an n+2n+2-gon, that is, Varπ⁡f≤tn​ℰπ​(f)\operatorname{Var}_{\pi}f\leq t_{n}\mathcal{E}_{\pi}(f) for all real-valued functions ff, and tnt_{n} is the smallest such constant.

Recall that, by the total law of variance, we may write

Varπ⁡f=Varπ¯⁡F+𝔼t∼π¯​Varπt​f.\operatorname{Var}_{\pi}f=\operatorname{Var}_{\overline{\pi}}F+\mathbb{E}_{t\sim\overline{\pi}}\operatorname{Var}_{\pi_{t}}f\,. (4.13)

By Lemma 4.4,

Varπ¯⁡F≤C′​(logc′⁡n)​n2​ℰπ​(f,f)=:h⁡(n)​ℰπ​(f),\operatorname{Var}_{\overline{\pi}}F\leq C^{\prime}(\log^{c^{\prime}}n)n^{2}\mathcal{E}_{\pi}(f,f)=:h(n)\mathcal{E}_{\pi}(f)\,, (4.14)

for some constants C′,c′>0C^{\prime},c^{\prime}>0.

To bound 𝔼t∼π¯​Varπt​f\mathbb{E}_{t\sim\overline{\pi}}\operatorname{Var}_{\pi_{t}}f recall that (Ωt,Pt)(\Omega_{t},P_{t}) is a product chain of at most three chains, each of which is the triangulation flip walk on a smaller polygon each of which has i+2i+2 sides for some i≤n/2i\leq n/2 (Lemma 4.1) Hence, by Lemma 2.5,

Varπt⁡f≤n−4i1−1​ti1​ℰπt​(f),\operatorname{Var}_{\pi_{t}}f\leq\frac{n-4}{i_{1}-1}t_{i_{1}}\mathcal{E}_{\pi_{t}}(f)\,, (4.15)

for some i1≤n/2i_{1}\leq n/2. Plugging in (4.14) and (4.15) into (4.13) we get

Varπ⁡f≤h⁡(n)​ℰπ​(f)+n−4i1−1​ti1​𝔼t∼πt​ℰπt​(f).\operatorname{Var}_{\pi}f\leq h(n)\mathcal{E}_{\pi}(f)+\frac{n-4}{i_{1}-1}t_{i_{1}}\mathbb{E}_{t\sim\pi_{t}}\mathcal{E}_{\pi_{t}}(f)\,. (4.16)

Recall that by the definition of the restriction chain (Ωt,Pt)(\Omega_{t},P_{t}), πt​(x)=π⁡(x)π¯​(t)\pi_{t}(x)=\frac{\pi(x)}{\overline{\pi}(t)} and

Pt​(x,y)=P⁡(x,y)∑z∈ΩtP⁡(x,z)=n−1n−4​P​(x,y),P_{t}(x,y)=\frac{P(x,y)}{\sum_{z\in\Omega_{t}}P(x,z)}=\frac{n-1}{n-4}P(x,y)\,,

for all x,y∈Ωtx,y\in\Omega_{t}. Thus,

𝔼t∼πt​ℰπt​(f)\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{t\sim\pi_{t}}\mathcal{E}_{\pi_{t}}(f) =∑t∈Ω¯π¯​(t)​∑x,y∈Ωtπt​(x)​Pt​(x,y)​(f⁡(x)−f⁡(y))2\displaystyle=\sum_{t\in\overline{\Omega}}\overline{\pi}(t)\sum_{x,y\in\Omega_{t}}\pi_{t}(x)P_{t}(x,y)(f(x)-f(y))^{2}
=n−1n−4​∑t∈Ω¯∑x,y∈Ωtπ⁡(x)​P​(x,y)​(f⁡(x)−f⁡(y))2\displaystyle=\frac{n-1}{n-4}\sum_{t\in\overline{\Omega}}\sum_{x,y\in\Omega_{t}}\pi(x)P(x,y)(f(x)-f(y))^{2}
≤n−1n−4​ℰπ​(f).\displaystyle\leq\frac{n-1}{n-4}\mathcal{E}_{\pi}(f)\,. (4.17)

Combining (4.16) and (4.17) we get that for all functions ff

Varπ⁡f≤[h⁡(n)+n−1i1−1​ti1]​ℰπ​(f),\operatorname{Var}_{\pi}f\leq\left[h(n)+\frac{n-1}{i_{1}-1}t_{i_{1}}\right]\mathcal{E}_{\pi}(f), (4.18)

i.e.

tn≤h⁡(n)+n−1i1−1​ti1,t_{n}\leq h(n)+\frac{n-1}{i_{1}-1}t_{i_{1}}\,, (4.19)

for some i1≤n/2i_{1}\leq n/2. Iterating this M≤log⁡nM\leq\log n times to reach the relaxation time of a constant-size walk, we get

≤h⁡(n)+n−1i1−1​h​(i1)+⋯+n−1iM−1​h​(iM)+n−1iM−1.\displaystyle\leq h(n)+\frac{n-1}{i_{1}-1}h(i_{1})+\dots+\frac{n-1}{i_{M}-1}h(i_{M})+\frac{n-1}{i_{M}-1}.

For the log-Sobolev inequality, the proof is nearly identical. Let g:=f2g:=f^{2} and t~n\tilde{t}_{n} be the inverse log-Sobolev constant for the flip walk on an n+2n+2-gon, that is, Entπ⁡g≤t~n​ℰπ​(f)\operatorname{Ent}_{\pi}g\leq\tilde{t}_{n}\mathcal{E}_{\pi}(f) for all non-constant functions ff, and t~n\tilde{t}_{n} is the smallest such constant. Entπ¯⁡G≤C′′​(logc′′⁡n)​n2​ℰπ​(f):=h~​(n)​ℰπ​(f).\operatorname{Ent}_{\overline{\pi}}G\leq C^{\prime\prime}(\log^{c^{\prime\prime}}n)n^{2}\mathcal{E}_{\pi}(f):=\tilde{h}(n)\mathcal{E}_{\pi}(f). (4.21)

t~n≤(log⁡n+1)​h~​(n)+n=O~​(n2),\tilde{t}_{n}\leq(\log n+1)\tilde{h}(n)+n=\widetilde{O}(n^{2}),

thus proving the desired log-Sobolev inequality. ∎

Corollary 1.2 follows immediately from Theorem 1.1 and the observation that the holding probability of the flip walk is 1/21/2.

5 A Transport Flow for Triangulations

5.1 Transport Flow Idea

In this section we describe and analyze the transport flow that will enable us to establish Lemma 4.8, the remaining ingredient in proving Theorem 1.1.

[EF23] gave a flow construction in combinatorial terms — a multi-way single-commodity flow (MSF) in their language. They gave a bound on the maximum congestion, which we will also use. For our purposes, we will also need a bound on the average congestion or the average path length in this construction (by [Mon14] these are equivalent), which is not immediate from their analysis. In this section we retrace their construction rigorously and establish the bounds we need to prove Theorem 1.1. To this end, we characterize the flow as a functional equality (not inequality)—in the spirit of [DS91]. In intuitive terms, we describe the problem of sending flow between a pair of states i,j∈Ω^i,j\in\hat{\Omega} as the difference F⁡(i)−F⁡(j)F(i)-F(j) in the value of the function FF at these two states (Lemma 5.1). We then describe the flow construction as an expectation of telescoping sums of differences over the paths in the flow. This formal description of the flow will allow us to analyze the average congestion in Section 6.

Lemma 5.1.

Let f:Ω→ℝf:\Omega\rightarrow\mathbb{R} be a function and consider the function FF. For all i,j∈Ω^,i,j\in\hat{\Omega}, there exists a flow function ϕi​j:{(x,y)∈(Ωi∪Ωj)2∣P⁡(x,y)>0}→ℝ\phi_{ij}:\left\{(x,y)\in(\Omega_{i}\cup\Omega_{j})^{2}\mid P(x,y)>0\right\}\rightarrow\mathbb{R} satisfying

F⁡(i)−F⁡(j)\displaystyle F(i)-F(j) =Δ2​π^​(i)​π^​(j)​∑x,y∈Ωiϕi​j,x​y​π​(x)​P​(x,y)​(f⁡(x)−f⁡(y))\displaystyle=\frac{\Delta}{2\hat{\pi}(i)\hat{\pi}(j)}\sum_{x,y\in\Omega_{i}}\phi_{ij,xy}\pi(x)P(x,y)(f(x)-f(y))
+Δ2​π^​(i)​π^​(j)∑x,y∈Ωjϕi​j,x​yπ(x)P(x,y)(f(x)−f(y))\displaystyle\qquad+\frac{\Delta}{2\hat{\pi}(i)\hat{\pi}(j)}\sum_{x,y\in\Omega_{j}}\phi_{ij,xy}\pi(x)P(x,y)(f(x)-f(y)) (5.1)
+Δπ^​(i)​π^​(j)∑x∈Ωi,y∈Ωjϕi​j,x​yπ(x)P(x,y)(f(x)−f(y)).\displaystyle\qquad+\frac{\Delta}{\hat{\pi}(i)\hat{\pi}(j)}\sum_{x\in\Omega_{i},y\in\Omega_{j}}\phi_{ij,xy}\pi(x)P(x,y)(f(x)-f(y))\,. (5.2)

where the function ϕi​j\phi_{ij} describes the congestion across the edge (x,y)(x,y), and where ϕi​j,x​y\phi_{ij,xy} is bounded in absolute value by 1.

(From our definition of ϕi​j\phi_{ij} it will follow that ϕi​j,x​y=−ϕi​j,y​x\phi_{ij,xy}=-\phi_{ij,yx} for all x,yx,y, so ϕi​j,x​y​(f⁡(x)−f⁡(y))=ϕi​j,y​x​(f⁡(y)−f⁡(x))\phi_{ij,xy}(f(x)-f(y))=\phi_{ij,yx}(f(y)-f(x)).)

The function ϕi​j\phi_{ij} induces a transport flow ΓΩi→Ωj\Gamma^{\Omega_{i}\rightarrow\Omega_{j}} in Ω\Omega that produces maximum congestion at most Δ\Delta.

In combinatorial terms, Lemma 5.1 describes a flow construction in which we route flow from Ωi\Omega_{i} to Ωj\Omega_{j}, through the state space of the overall chain. The congestion incurred by this flow is at most Δ\Delta.

In this section, we will prove Lemma 5.1. In Section 6, combining Lemma 5.1 with an additional average congestion analysis relying on the asymptotic behavior of Catalan structures, we will then prove the following:

Lemma 5.2.

For all S,T⊆Ω^,S,T\subseteq\hat{\Omega}, there exists a transport flow ΓΩ⁡[S]→Ω⁡[T]\Gamma^{\Omega[S]\rightarrow\Omega[T]} in Ω\Omega that produces maximum congestion ρ≤Δ\rho\leq\Delta and that satisfies ρ¯Ω⁡[S]≤C​logc​n⋅n​π^​(T)\bar{\rho}_{\Omega[S]}\leq C\log^{c}n\cdot\sqrt{n}\hat{\pi}(T) and ρ¯Ω⁡[T]≤C​logc​n⋅n​π^​(S)\bar{\rho}_{\Omega[T]}\leq C\log^{c}n\cdot\sqrt{n}\hat{\pi}(S) for constants C>0,c>0C>0,c>0.33 3 In Lemma 4.8 we considered sets S,T⊆ΩS,T\subseteq\Omega that were subsets of the overall state space. Here we have redefined S,T⊆Ω^S,T\subseteq\hat{\Omega}, as this will be convenient in the proofs in Section 6. Thus we are using the notation Ω⁡[S],Ω⁡[T]\Omega[S],\Omega[T] (which we defined in Section 2) to denote the induced subsets of the overall state space Ω\Omega.

Lemma 5.2 strengthens Lemma 5.1 in two ways: adding an average congestion analysis, and allowing for the sets S,TS,T in the transport flow to include multiple states in the projection chain. Once proven, Lemma 5.2 will imply Lemma 4.8, which completes the proof of Theorem 1.1 given in Section 4.

5.2 Pinnings

Our aim is now to prove Lemma 5.1. We need to adapt the idea of a pinning from existing local-to-global frameworks. However, our case involves a recursive partitioning of the state space, rather than a simplicial complex. We will define a pinning to be a sequence η=(i1,i2,…,is)\eta=(i_{1},i_{2},\dots,i_{s}) of polygon vertices, where no j<j′<j′′j<j^{\prime}<j^{\prime\prime} triple exists such that ij′<ij<ij′′i_{j^{\prime}}<i_{j}<i_{j^{\prime\prime}} or ij′′<ij<ij′i_{j^{\prime\prime}}<i_{j}<i_{j^{\prime}}. The pinning induces a collection of triangles which we construct recursively: we begin with the triangle (0,n+1,i1)(0,n+1,i_{1}), then for every 2≤j≤s2\leq j\leq s, we add the unique triangle that includes vertex iji_{j} as well as some edge already added to the pinning. See Figure 4.

Let Ωη\Omega_{\eta} be the set of triangulations x∈Ωx\in\Omega such that xx contains the triangles induced by the pinning η\eta. The “innermost” triangle TT of η\eta (the one having the last vertex of η\eta as a vertex) induces a split of part of the nn-gon into left and right sides, see Figure 5. Each state x∈Ωηx\in\Omega_{\eta} has one or two triangles sharing an edge with TT. Define Ω^η,l\hat{\Omega}_{\eta,l} and respectively Ω^η,r\hat{\Omega}_{\eta,r} to be the projection chains induced by identifying each state x∈Ωηx\in\Omega_{\eta} with its triangles to the left and right of TT. (In Fig. 5, Ω^η,l={i3+1,i3+2,…,i4−1}\hat{\Omega}_{\eta,l}=\{i_{3}+1,i_{3}+2,\dots,i_{4}-1\} and Ω^η,r={i4+1,i4+2,…,i2−1}\hat{\Omega}_{\eta,r}=\{i_{4}+1,i_{4}+2,\dots,i_{2}-1\}. In Fig. 6, we zoom in to the equivalence classes that form the projection chain Ω^η,l\hat{\Omega}_{\eta,l}.)

Given a pinning η=(i1,i2,…,ik)\eta=(i_{1},i_{2},\dots,i_{k}), let π^​(η)=π​(Ωη)\hat{\pi}(\eta)=\pi(\Omega_{\eta}). Given a vertex j∈Ω^η,l∪Ω^η,rj\in\hat{\Omega}_{\eta,l}\cup{\hat{\Omega}}_{\eta,r}, let η​j\eta j be the pinning (i1,i2,…,ik,j)(i_{1},i_{2},\dots,i_{k},j). In general, writing a string of pinnings and/or vertices will denote the pinning derived by concatenating the elements of the string. E.g. Ωi​j​k\Omega_{ijk} where i,j,k∈Ω^i,j,k\in\hat{\Omega} is equivalent to Ωη\Omega_{\eta} where η=(i,j,k)\eta=(i,j,k). Let π^η​(j)=π⁡(Ωη​j)π⁡(Ωη)\hat{\pi}_{\eta}(j)=\frac{\pi(\Omega_{\eta j})}{\pi(\Omega_{\eta})}.

When considering a function f:Ω→ℝf:\Omega\rightarrow\mathbb{R} we will write F​(η)=𝔼πη​[f]F(\eta)=\mathbb{E}_{\pi_{\eta}}[f].

If 0≤k<l0\leq k<l then

The ratios being compared in Lemma 5.5 will determine the congestion incurred across certain sets of edges in our transport flow. For every pinning η\eta and for all i,j∈Ω^η,li,j\in\hat{\Omega}_{\eta,l} (similarly for all i,j∈Ω^η,ri,j\in\hat{\Omega}_{\eta,r}), there is a perfect matching between Ωη​i​j\Omega_{\eta ij} and Ωη​j​i\Omega_{\eta ji}.

Lemma 5.8.

Let η\eta be a pinning. Suppose i,j∈Ω^η,li,j\in\hat{\Omega}_{\eta,l} or i,j∈Ω^η,ri,j\in\hat{\Omega}_{\eta,r}. Suppose j>ij>i without loss of generality. Then

F⁡(η​i)−F⁡(η​i​j)\displaystyle F(\eta i)-F(\eta ij) =∑k∈Ω^η​i,rπ^η​i​(k)​(F⁡(η​i​k)−F⁡(η​i​j)).\displaystyle=\sum_{k\in\hat{\Omega}_{\eta i,r}}\hat{\pi}_{\eta i}(k)(F(\eta ik)-F(\eta ij))\,. (5.4)
Proof.

Using the definition of F⁡(⋅)F(\cdot) and π^(⋅)​(⋅)\hat{\pi}_{(\cdot)}(\cdot) we obtain the identities F⁡(η​i)=∑k∈Ω^η​i,rπ^η​i​(k)​F​(η​i​k)F(\eta i)~=~\sum_{k\in\hat{\Omega}_{\eta i,r}}~\hat{\pi}_{\eta i}(k)F(\eta ik) and ∑k∈Ω^η​i,rπ^η​i​(k)=1\sum_{k\in\hat{\Omega}_{\eta i,r}}\hat{\pi}_{\eta i}(k)=1. (5.4) follows. ∎

In the proof of Lemma 5.1 we will construct a flow in which states in Ωi\Omega_{i} send flow to states in Ωj\Omega_{j}. In this flow, a commodity is initially uniformly distributed throughout Ωi\Omega_{i} and must be sent along edges (transitions) in the state space Ω\Omega so that it is uniformly distributed throughout Ωj\Omega_{j}. The expression

π^​(i)​π^​(j)​(F⁡(i)−F⁡(j))\hat{\pi}(i)\hat{\pi}(j)(F(i)-F(j))

captures the “problem” of routing this flow from Ωi\Omega_{i} to Ωj\Omega_{j}. Constructing a flow is equivalent to decomposing this expression into a summation over expressions

ϕi​j,x​y​π​(x)​P​(x,y)​(f⁡(x)−f⁡(y))orϕj​i,x​y​π​(x)​P​(x,y)​(f⁡(x)−f⁡(y)),\phi_{ij,xy}\pi(x)P(x,y)(f(x)-f(y))\quad\textrm{or}\quad\phi_{ji,xy}\pi(x)P(x,y)(f(x)-f(y))\,,

with ϕi​j,x​y\phi_{ij,xy} (or ϕj​i,x​y\phi_{ji,xy}) giving the flow across each (x,y)(x,y) edge (and thus Δ​ϕi​j,x​y\Delta\phi_{ij,xy} or Δ​ϕj​i,x​y\Delta\phi_{ji,xy} giving the congestion across each edge). In fact, the ϕi​j,x​y\phi_{ij,xy}, ϕj​i,x​y\phi_{ji,xy} values will obey the axioms of an Ωi\Omega_{i}-Ωj\Omega_{j} flow as described in Section 2.5.

I.e. the net flow out of each x∈Ωix\in\Omega_{i} will be π⁡(x)​π^​(j)\pi(x)\hat{\pi}(j), the net flow into each y∈Ωjy\in\Omega_{j} will be π^​(i)​π​(y)\hat{\pi}(i)\pi(y), i.e.

∑y∼xϕi​j,x​y=π⁡(x)​π^​(j),\sum_{y\sim x}\phi_{ij,xy}=\pi(x)\hat{\pi}(j)\,,

for all x∈Ωix\in\Omega_{i} and

∑x∼yϕj​i,x​y=π^​(i)​π​(y),\sum_{x\sim y}\phi_{ji,xy}=\hat{\pi}(i)\pi(y)\,,

for all y∈Ωjy\in\Omega_{j}.

Also, we will have ϕi​j,x​y=−ϕi​j,y​x\phi_{ij,xy}=-\phi_{ij,yx}.

The way we will accomplish this decomposition is to recursively decompose Ω\Omega by first partitioning using the projection chain Ω^\hat{\Omega}, then recursively decomposing Ωi\Omega_{i} for each i∈Ω^i\in\hat{\Omega}.

Definition 5.9.

Given η=(k1=i,k2,…,kd)\eta=(k_{1}=i,k_{2},\dots,k_{d}) define a function ϕi​j,η​s​t\phi_{ij,\eta st} recursively so that:

  • •

    ϕi​j,i​j=π^​(j)π^i​(j)\phi_{ij,ij}=\frac{\hat{\pi}(j)}{\hat{\pi}_{i}(j)} ,

  • •

    ϕj​i,j​i=−ϕi​j,i​j\phi_{ji,ji}=-\phi_{ij,ij} ,

  • •

    ϕi​j,i​j′=0\phi_{ij,ij^{\prime}}=0 for all j′≠jj^{\prime}\neq j, and

  • •

    ϕj​i,j​i′=0\phi_{ji,ji^{\prime}}=0 for all i′≠ii^{\prime}\neq i .

For all s,t∈Ω^η,ls,t\in\hat{\Omega}_{\eta,l} (similarly for all s,t∈Ω^η,rs,t\in\hat{\Omega}_{\eta,r}) let

ϕi​j,η​s​t=π^η​(t)π^η​s​(t)​(ϕi​j,η​t−ϕi​j,η​s)=π^η​(s)π^η​t​(s)​(ϕi​j,η​t−ϕi​j,η​s),\displaystyle\phi_{ij,\eta st}=\frac{\hat{\pi}_{\eta}(t)}{\hat{\pi}_{\eta s}(t)}(\phi_{ij,\eta t}-\phi_{ij,\eta s})=\frac{\hat{\pi}_{\eta}(s)}{\hat{\pi}_{\eta t}(s)}(\phi_{ij,\eta t}-\phi_{ij,\eta s})\,, (5.5)

and whenever η′=η​kd+1\eta^{\prime}=\eta k_{d+1} let ϕi​j,η′​s=ϕi​j,η​kd+1​s\phi_{ij,\eta^{\prime}s}=\phi_{ij,\eta k_{d+1}s}.

For all x∈Ωη​s​t,y∈Ωη​t​sx\in\Omega_{\eta st},y\in\Omega_{\eta ts} let ϕi​j,x​y=ϕi​j,η​s​t\phi_{ij,xy}=\phi_{ij,\eta st}.

Finally, for x∈Ωi,y∈Ωj,P⁡(x,y)>0x\in\Omega_{i},y\in\Omega_{j},P(x,y)>0, let ϕi​j,x​y=ϕi​j,i​j\phi_{ij,xy}=\phi_{ij,ij}.

This function will describe the flow across each edge in our construction. In particular, ϕη​s​t\phi_{\eta st} describes the flow across edges (x,y)(x,y) where x∈Ωη​s,y∈Ωη​tx\in\Omega_{\eta s},y\in\Omega_{\eta t}.

Conceptually, at each step of the decomposition, we are within some Ωη\Omega_{\eta}. We imagine that ϕi​j,η​s\phi_{ij,\eta s} flow is concentrated within states in {Ωη​s∣s∈Ω^η,l}\{\Omega_{\eta s}\mid s\in\hat{\Omega}_{\eta,l}\} (and similarly for Ω^η,r\hat{\Omega}_{\eta,r}), which must be distributed to the rest of Ωη\Omega_{\eta}. This reduces to the problem of distributing the flow to each Ωη​t,t∈Ω^η,l\Omega_{\eta t},t\in\hat{\Omega}_{\eta,l}. The resulting flow across the matching Ωη​s​t,Ωη​t​s\Omega_{\eta st},\Omega_{\eta ts} is precisely

ϕi​j,η​s⋅π^η​(s)​π^η​(t)π^η​(s​t)\displaystyle\phi_{ij,\eta s}\cdot\frac{\hat{\pi}_{\eta}(s)\hat{\pi}_{\eta}(t)}{\hat{\pi}_{\eta}(st)} =ϕi​j,η​s⋅π^η​(t)π^η​s​(t)=ϕi​j,η​s⋅π^η​(s)π^η​t​(s).\displaystyle=\phi_{ij,\eta s}\cdot\frac{\hat{\pi}_{\eta}(t)}{\hat{\pi}_{\eta s}(t)}=\phi_{ij,\eta s}\cdot\frac{\hat{\pi}_{\eta}(s)}{\hat{\pi}_{\eta t}(s)}\,. (5.6)

This is because the total flow concentrated in Ωη​s\Omega_{\eta s} is ϕi​j,η​s​π^​(η)​π^η​(s)\phi_{ij,\eta s}\hat{\pi}(\eta)\hat{\pi}_{\eta}(s), and a π^η​(t)\hat{\pi}_{\eta}(t) portion of this flow must be sent to Ωη​t\Omega_{\eta t}. Distributing this flow across the edges in the matching (Ωη​s​t,Ωη​t​s)(\Omega_{\eta st},\Omega_{\eta ts}), each side of which has measure π^​(η)​π^η​(s​t)\hat{\pi}(\eta)\hat{\pi}_{\eta}(st), justifies the left-hand side of (5.6). The right-hand side follows from the definition of π^(⋅)​(⋅)\hat{\pi}_{(\cdot)}(\cdot).

We obtain (5.5) from considering the symmetric problem of distributing flow from Ωη​t\Omega_{\eta t} to Ωη​s\Omega_{\eta s}.

Before presenting the formal construction, we prove the following lemmas.

Lemma 5.10.

For all i,j∈Ω^i,j\in\hat{\Omega}, for all pinnings η=(i=k1,k2,…,kd)\eta=(i=k_{1},k_{2},\dots,k_{d}) such that j∼ηj\sim\eta,

Lemma 5.11.

For all i,j∈Ω^i,j\in\hat{\Omega}, for all pinnings η=(i=k1,k2,…,kd)\eta=(i=k_{1},k_{2},\dots,k_{d}) such that j=kuj=k_{u} for some u∈[d]u\in[d], and for all s,t∈Ω^η,rs,t\in\hat{\Omega}_{\eta,r} where s<ts<t (similarly for all s,t∈Ω^η,ls,t\in\hat{\Omega}_{\eta,l} where t<st<s): either

0≤ϕi​j,η​s≤ϕi​j,η​t≤10\leq\phi_{ij,\eta s}\leq\phi_{ij,\eta t}\leq 1 (5.7)

or

0≥ϕi​j,η​s≥ϕi​j,η​t≥−1.0\geq\phi_{ij,\eta s}\geq\phi_{ij,\eta t}\geq-1\,. (5.8)

=π^τ′​(s)π^τ′​j​(s)​(ϕi​j,τ′​s−ϕi​j,τ′​j)\displaystyle=\frac{\hat{\pi}_{\tau^{\prime}}(s)}{\hat{\pi}_{\tau^{\prime}j}(s)}(\phi_{ij,\tau^{\prime}s}-\phi_{ij,\tau^{\prime}j}) (5.10)
=−π^​(j)π^τ′​(j)⋅π^τ′​(s)π^τ′​j​(s).\displaystyle=-\frac{\hat{\pi}(j)}{\hat{\pi}_{\tau^{\prime}}(j)}\cdot\frac{\hat{\pi}_{\tau^{\prime}}(s)}{\hat{\pi}_{\tau^{\prime}j}(s)}\,. (5.11)

To prove Lemma 5.1, we will introduce the following notation for convenience:

Definition 5.12.

Given a pinning η\eta and given s,t∈Ω^η,ls,t\in\hat{\Omega}_{\eta,l} (similarly given s,t∈Ω^η,rs,t\in\hat{\Omega}_{\eta,r}) define the following:

  • •

    Let Fη​s→η​t=π^​(η)​π^η​(s)​π^η​(t)​(F⁡(η​s)−F⁡(η​t))F_{\eta s\rightarrow\eta t}=\hat{\pi}(\eta)\hat{\pi}_{\eta}(s)\hat{\pi}_{\eta}(t)(F(\eta s)-F(\eta t)).

  • •

    Let Fη​s​t→η​t​s=π^​(η)​π^η​(s)​π^η​s​(t)​(F⁡(η​s​t)−F⁡(η​t​s))F_{\eta st\rightarrow\eta ts}=\hat{\pi}(\eta)\hat{\pi}_{\eta}(s)\hat{\pi}_{\eta s}(t)(F(\eta st)-F(\eta ts)).
