Intuitively, Fη​s→η​tF_{\eta s\rightarrow\eta t} is a term that describes the weighted difference of FF between η​s\eta s and η​t\eta t.

Proof of Lemma 5.1.

Recall that our goal is to send the flow Fi→jF_{i\rightarrow j} from Ωi\Omega_{i} to Ωj\Omega_{j} and bound its congestion. The main idea is that, by an appropriate rerouting and decomposition of the flow, the original problem is reduced to a set of equivalent problems of smaller size. A recursive application of this idea will result in the proof of the lemma.

We begin by applying the flow rerouting Ωi→Ωi​j→Ωj​i→Ωj\Omega_{i}\rightarrow\Omega_{ij}\rightarrow\Omega_{ji}\rightarrow\Omega_{j} to get

Fi→j\displaystyle F_{i\rightarrow j} =ϕi​j,i​j​Fi→i​j\displaystyle=\phi_{ij,ij}F_{i\rightarrow ij}
+ϕi​j,i​j​Fi​j→j​i\displaystyle\qquad+\phi_{ij,ij}F_{ij\rightarrow ji}
+ϕi​j,i​j​Fj​i→j\displaystyle\qquad+\phi_{ij,ij}F_{ji\rightarrow j}
=ϕi​j,i​j​Fi→i​j\displaystyle=\phi_{ij,ij}F_{i\rightarrow ij} (5.16)
+ϕi​j,i​j​Fi​j→j​i\displaystyle\qquad+\phi_{ij,ij}F_{ij\rightarrow ji} (5.17)
+ϕj​i,j​i​Fj→j​i\displaystyle\qquad+\phi_{ji,ji}F_{j\rightarrow ji} (5.18)

(and note ϕi​j,i​j=π^​(j)π^i​(j)=π^​(i)π^j​(i)=−ϕj​i,j​i\phi_{ij,ij}=\frac{\hat{\pi}(j)}{\hat{\pi}_{i}(j)}=\frac{\hat{\pi}(i)}{\hat{\pi}_{j}(i)}=-\phi_{ji,ji}, so (5.17) is in fact symmetrically consistent).

First we consider (5.17). By Lemma 5.7, we immediately get

π^​(j)π^i​(j)​Fi​j→j​i=∑x∈Ωi,y∈ΩjΔ​ϕi​j,x​y​π​(x)​P​(x,y)​(f⁡(x)−f⁡(y)),\frac{\hat{\pi}(j)}{\hat{\pi}_{i}(j)}F_{ij\rightarrow ji}\ =\sum_{x\in\Omega_{i},y\in\Omega_{j}}\Delta\phi_{ij,xy}\pi(x)P(x,y)\left(f(x)-f(y)\right)\,, (5.19)

where 0≤ϕi​j,x​y=ϕi​j,i​j=π^​(j)π^i​(j)≤1.0\leq\phi_{ij,xy}=\phi_{ij,ij}=\frac{\hat{\pi}(j)}{\hat{\pi}_{i}(j)}\leq 1.

Next we observe that (5.16) and (5.18) are symmetric. Thus it suffices to consider (5.16). Without loss of generality assume j>ij>i. Every triangulation in Ωi\Omega_{i} has to triangulate Ωi,r\Omega_{i,r} and thus we can apply the flow decomposition ∪k∈Ω^i,rΩi​k→Ωi​j\cup_{k\in\hat{\Omega}_{i,r}}\Omega_{ik}\rightarrow\Omega_{ij} to get

π^​(j)π^i​(j)​Fi→i​j=π^​(j)π^i​(j)​∑k∈Ω^i,rFi​k→i​j=∑k∈Ω^i,rϕi​j,i​j​Fi​k→i​j.\frac{\hat{\pi}(j)}{\hat{\pi}_{i}(j)}F_{i\rightarrow ij}=\frac{\hat{\pi}(j)}{\hat{\pi}_{i}(j)}\sum_{k\in\hat{\Omega}_{i,r}}F_{ik\rightarrow ij}=\sum_{k\in\hat{\Omega}_{i,r}}\phi_{ij,ij}F_{ik\rightarrow ij}\,. (5.20)

Note that the problem of sending flow from Ωi​k\Omega_{ik} to Ωi​j\Omega_{ij} can be viewed as the problem of sending flow from “Ωk\Omega_{k}” to “Ωj\Omega_{j}” in the smaller polygon that has i​0i0 as a side and contains k,jk,j. We thus repeat the equivalent rerouting as the one in the beginning of the proof, that is Ωi​k→Ωi​k​j→Ωi​j​k→Ωi​j\Omega_{ik}\rightarrow\Omega_{ikj}\rightarrow\Omega_{ijk}\rightarrow\Omega_{ij} to get

Fi​k→i​j\displaystyle F_{ik\rightarrow ij} =π^i​(j)π^i​k​(j)​Fi​k→i​k​j+π^i​(j)π^i​k​(j)​Fi​k​j→i​j​k+π^i​(k)π^i​j​(k)​Fi​j​k→i​j.\displaystyle=\frac{\hat{\pi}_{i}(j)}{\hat{\pi}_{ik}(j)}F_{ik\rightarrow ikj}+\frac{\hat{\pi}_{i}(j)}{\hat{\pi}_{ik}(j)}F_{ikj\rightarrow ijk}+\frac{\hat{\pi}_{i}(k)}{\hat{\pi}_{ij}(k)}F_{ijk\rightarrow ij}\,. (5.21)

Substituting (5.21) into (5.20) we get

π^​(j)π^i​(j)​Fi→i​j\displaystyle\frac{\hat{\pi}(j)}{\hat{\pi}_{i}(j)}F_{i\rightarrow ij} =π^​(j)π^i​(j)​∑k∈Ω^i,r[π^i​(j)π^i​k​(j)​Fi​k→i​k​j+π^i​(j)π^i​k​(j)​Fi​k​j→i​j​k+π^i​(j)π^i​k​(j)​Fi​j​k→i​j]\displaystyle=\frac{\hat{\pi}(j)}{\hat{\pi}_{i}(j)}\sum_{k\in\hat{\Omega}_{i,r}}\left[\frac{\hat{\pi}_{i}(j)}{\hat{\pi}_{ik}(j)}F_{ik\rightarrow ikj}+\frac{\hat{\pi}_{i}(j)}{\hat{\pi}_{ik}(j)}F_{ikj\rightarrow ijk}+\frac{\hat{\pi}_{i}(j)}{\hat{\pi}_{ik}(j)}F_{ijk\rightarrow ij}\right]
=∑k∈Ω^i,rϕi​j,i​k​j​Fi​k→i​k​j\displaystyle=\sum_{k\in\hat{\Omega}_{i,r}}\phi_{ij,ikj}F_{ik\rightarrow ikj} (5.22)
+∑k∈Ω^i,rϕi​j,i​k​jFi​k​j→i​j​k\displaystyle\qquad+\sum_{k\in\hat{\Omega}_{i,r}}\phi_{ij,ikj}F_{ikj\rightarrow ijk} (5.23)
+∑k∈Ω^i,rϕi​j,i​j​kFi​j→i​j​k.\displaystyle\qquad+\sum_{k\in\hat{\Omega}_{i,r}}\phi_{ij,ijk}F_{ij\rightarrow ijk}\,. (5.24)

Observe that, again, there is a clear analogy between the pairs of equations (5.22)-(5.16), (5.23)-(5.17), (5.24)-(5.18).

Iterating the previous steps, one obtains a decomposition of the original term Fi→i​jF_{i\rightarrow ij} into expressions of the form (5.23)-(5.17). To prove the lemma, it suffices to bound the coefficients ϕi​j,x​y\phi_{ij,xy} on the right-hand side.

Furthermore, this decomposition preserves the invariant that the coefficient of the term Fi→i​jF_{i\rightarrow ij} in (5.17)—and similarly Fi​k​j→i​j​kF_{ikj\rightarrow ijk} in (5.23) and all other terms of the same form—is bounded in absolute value by one.

In general, the coefficients are of the form

ϕi​j,η​s​t=π^η​(t)π^η​s​(t)​(ϕi​j,η​t−ϕi​j,η​s)\phi_{ij,\eta st}=\frac{\hat{\pi}_{\eta}(t)}{\hat{\pi}_{\eta s}(t)}(\phi_{ij,\eta t}-\phi_{ij,\eta s}) (5.25)

(as in the definition) , which is bounded in absolute value by one, by Eq. 5.8.

(5.25) can be justified as follows: first, note the coefficient ϕi​j,x​y=ϕi​j,i​j=π^​(j)π^i​(j)\phi_{ij,xy}=\phi_{ij,ij}=\frac{\hat{\pi}(j)}{\hat{\pi}_{i}(j)} in (5.17).

For a given η\eta and η′=η​u\eta^{\prime}=\eta u, and for a given s,t∈Ω^η′,rs,t\in\hat{\Omega}_{\eta^{\prime},r}, the term Fη′​s→η′​tF_{\eta^{\prime}s\rightarrow\eta^{\prime}t} arises from equalities of the following form

∑tϕi​j,η​t​Fη→η​t\displaystyle\sum_{t}\phi_{ij,\eta t}F_{\eta\rightarrow\eta t} =∑t∑sϕi​j,η​t​Fη​s→η​t\displaystyle=\sum_{t}\sum_{s}\phi_{ij,\eta t}F_{\eta s\rightarrow\eta t}
=∑s,t:s<t(ϕi​j,η​t−ϕi​j,η​s)Fη​s→η​t\displaystyle=\sum_{s,t:s<t}(\phi_{ij,\eta t}-\phi_{ij,\eta s})F_{\eta s\rightarrow\eta t}
=∑s,t:s<t(ϕi​j,η​t−ϕi​j,η​s)[π^η​(t)π^η​s​(t)Fη​s→η​s​t+π^η​(t)π^η​s​(t)Fη​s​t→η​t​s+π^η​(s)π^η​t​(s)Fη​t​s→η​t]\displaystyle=\sum_{s,t:s<t}(\phi_{ij,\eta t}-\phi_{ij,\eta s})\left[\frac{\hat{\pi}_{\eta}(t)}{\hat{\pi}_{\eta s}(t)}F_{\eta s\rightarrow\eta st}+\frac{\hat{\pi}_{\eta}(t)}{\hat{\pi}_{\eta s}(t)}F_{\eta st\rightarrow\eta ts}+\frac{\hat{\pi}_{\eta}(s)}{\hat{\pi}_{\eta t}(s)}F_{\eta ts\rightarrow\eta t}\right]
=∑s,t:s<t[ϕi​j,η​s​tFη​s→η​s​t+ϕi​j,η​s​tFη​s​t→η​t​s+ϕi​j,η​t​sFη​t→η​t​s].\displaystyle=\sum_{s,t:s<t}\left[\phi_{ij,\eta st}F_{\eta s\rightarrow\eta st}+\phi_{ij,\eta st}F_{\eta st\rightarrow\eta ts}+\phi_{ij,\eta ts}F_{\eta t\rightarrow\eta ts}\right]\,. (5.26)

The function ϕi​j\phi_{ij} describes the desired Ωi\Omega_{i}-Ωj\Omega_{j} flow. Furthermore, the maximum congestion is at most Δ\Delta since ϕi​j\phi_{ij} takes on values bounded in absolute value by one, and since P⁡(x,y)=1ΔP(x,y)=\frac{1}{\Delta} whenever P⁡(x,y)>0P(x,y)>0.. Finally, the existence of the desired transport flow follows from applying Lemma 3.4 to ϕi​j\phi_{ij}. ∎

6 Bounding the Maximum and Average Congestion

First we give a bound on the maximum congestion, which we will prove in Appendix B:

Lemma 6.1.

In the flow construction in Lemma 5.1, let x,y∈Ωx,y\in\Omega. Then

|∑i∈S,j∈Tϕi​j,x​y|≤1.\Bigl|\sum_{i\in S,j\in T}\phi_{ij,xy}\Bigr|\leq 1\,.

The rest of this section is devoted to proving a bound on the average congestion.

Given a triangulation pair x,yx,y satisfying P⁡(x,y)>0P(x,y)>0, there exists a unique maximal pinning η\eta such that x,y∈Ωηx,y\in\Omega_{\eta}. We will call this pinning ηx​y\eta_{xy}. See Fig. 8.

Given x∈Ωx\in\Omega, each diagonal in xx induces a transition to y∈Ωy\in\Omega, and thereby induces a pinning ηx​y\eta_{xy}. Furthermore, using the duality between Catalan triangulations and Catalan trees, let x∗x^{*} be the tree that corresponds to the triangulation xx. One can identify each diagonal in xx—and therefore each pinning ηx​y\eta_{xy}—with a tree edge in x∗x^{*} between a parent node and a child node. We will define dx​(η)=dx​(ηx​y)d_{x}(\eta)=d_{x}(\eta_{xy}) to be the depth of the child node of this tree edge.

Our strategy in this section will be as follows: let i,j∈Ω^i,j\in\hat{\Omega} be as in Lemma 5.1. We observe that given x∈Ωix\in\Omega_{i}, and given a pinning η=(k1=i,…,kd),\eta~=~(k_{1}=i,\dots,k_{d}), there are (at most) two additional pinnings η(l)=η​kd+1(l)\eta^{(l)}=\eta k_{d+1}^{(l)} and η(r)=η​kd+1(r)\eta^{(r)}=\eta k_{d+1}^{(r)} such that kd+1(l)∈Ω^η​lk_{d+1}^{(l)}\in\hat{\Omega}_{\eta l}, kd+1(r)∈Ω^η​rk_{d+1}^{(r)}\in\hat{\Omega}_{\eta r}, and x∈Ωη(l)x\in\Omega_{\eta^{(l)}} and x∈Ωη(r)x\in\Omega_{\eta^{(r)}}. See Fig. 9.

Given a pinning η\eta and a vertex k∈Ω^η​lk\in\hat{\Omega}_{\eta l} or k∈Ω^η​rk\in\hat{\Omega}_{\eta r}, let η′=η​k\eta^{\prime}=\eta k. Then given x∈Ωη′x\in\Omega_{\eta^{\prime}} define ϕi​j,η′(x)=ϕi​j,η​k\phi_{ij,\eta^{\prime}}^{(x)}=\phi_{ij,\eta k}—where ϕi​j,η​k\phi_{ij,\eta k} is the notation used in Lemma 5.1. We will show that given i∈S,j∈Ti\in S,j\in T, for each depth level dd we have

∑η:x∈Ωη,d⁡(η)=d|ϕi​j,η(x)|≤1.\sum_{\eta:x\in\Omega_{\eta},d(\eta)=d}|\phi_{ij,\eta}^{(x)}|\leq 1\,.

That is, the sum of the congestion values incurred in the flow in Lemma 5.1 across flips at a given level of (the dual tree of) a given triangulation x∈Ωix\in\Omega_{i} sums to at most one. Formally:

Lemma 6.2.

With the notation of Lemma 5.1, given i,j∈Ω^i,j\in\hat{\Omega} and given η=(k1=i,k2,…,kd)\eta=(k_{1}=i,k_{2},\dots,k_{d}) such that j∈ηj\in\eta, let

ϕi​j,l∗​(η)\displaystyle\phi_{ij,l}^{*}(\eta) =maxs∈Ω^η,l⁡{|ϕi​j,η​s|},\displaystyle=\max_{s\in\hat{\Omega}_{\eta,l}}\{|\phi_{ij,\eta s}|\},
ϕi​j,r∗​(η)\displaystyle\phi_{ij,r}^{*}(\eta) =maxs∈Ω^η,r⁡{|ϕi​j,η​s|}.\displaystyle=\max_{s\in\hat{\Omega}_{\eta,r}}\{|\phi_{ij,\eta s}|\}\,.

Then if η′=(k1,k2,…,kd,kd+1)\eta^{\prime}=(k_{1},k_{2},\dots,k_{d},k_{d+1}) where kd+1∈Ω^η,lk_{d+1}\in\hat{\Omega}_{\eta,l} then ϕi​j,l∗​(η′)+ϕi​j,r∗​(η′)≤ϕi​j,l∗​(η)\phi_{ij,l}^{*}(\eta^{\prime})+\phi_{ij,r}^{*}(\eta^{\prime})\leq\phi_{ij,l}^{*}(\eta), and the symmetric fact holds for kd+1∈Ω^η,rk_{d+1}\in\hat{\Omega}_{\eta,r}.

Then we will use the fact that when xx is a (uniformly random) triangulation drawn from π\pi, the expected depth of x∗x^{*} is O~​(n)\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{n}):

Lemma 6.3 ([Fla+93]).

The probability that a random Catalan tree on nn nodes has depth at least dd is

O(n3/2e−d2/(4n)).O\left(n^{3/2}e^{-d^{2}/(4n)}\right)\,.

The probability that a random Catalan tree on nn nodes has depth at most dd is

O(n3/2e−δn/d2),O\left(n^{3/2}e^{-\delta n/d^{2}}\right)\,,

for a constant δ>0\delta>0.

Lemma 6.4 ([MM78]).

There exist constants C>0C>0 and cc such that for sufficiently large nn, the probability that a uniformly chosen node in a uniformly chosen Catalan tree on nn nodes has depth dd is proportional to dd whenever d≤C​n​logc⁡nd\leq C\sqrt{n}\log^{c}n.

A straightforward consequence of Lemmas 6.3 and 6.4 is:

Corollary 6.5.

The expected depth of a random node in a random Catalan tree is Θ~​(n)\widetilde{\Theta}(\sqrt{n}).

We will use Corollary 6.5 to bound the total congestion incurred across edges in xx as the sum of congestion over O⁡(n)O(\sqrt{n}) levels, which in turn will be O⁡(n)O(\sqrt{n}) total congestion by Lemma 6.2. Since the transition probability in the flip walk between any adjacent x,yx,y pair is Θ⁡(1n)\Theta\left(\frac{1}{n}\right), this in turn will imply that the average congestion over the edges (transitions) incident to xx is O⁡(nn)O\left(\frac{\sqrt{n}}{n}\right). We state this in Lemma 6.6. Roughly speaking, this will, with some algebraic manipulation, enable the shaving of a Θ⁡(n)\Theta(\sqrt{n}) factor from our overall average congestion bound. More precisely, we will use Lemma 6.6 to prove Lemma 5.2.

Let 𝒯i​j\mathcal{T}_{ij} be the set of all triangles that have one vertex at jj and two other vertices on opposite sides of the special edge (i,n+1)(i,n+1) (see Fig. 10). Given a triangle t∈𝒯i​jt\in\mathcal{T}_{ij}, let Ωi​t:={x∈Ωi∣x​ includes the triangle ​t}\Omega_{it}:=\{x\in\Omega_{i}\mid x\textnormal{ includes the triangle }t\}. The triangle tt divides the polygon into three sub-polygons, bounded by the three sides of tt. Let li​(t)l_{i}(t) denote the size of the sub-polygon on the side bounded by the “base” of tt (the side closer to the special edge) and the edge (i,n+1)(i,n+1). Let ui​(t)u_{i}(t) denote the size of the larger of the other two sub-polygons.

Let d⁡(η)d(\eta) be the depth of (i.e. the number of triangles in) a given pinning η\eta. Given x∈Ωix\in\Omega_{i} let dj​(x)d_{j}(x) denote the depth of the unique pinning η\eta such that x∈Ωη​jx\in\Omega_{\eta j}. See Fig. 11.

Given a pinning η\eta and a vertex j∉ηj\notin\eta, let j∼ηj\sim\eta if j∈Ω^η,lj\in\hat{\Omega}_{\eta,l} or j∈Ω^η,rj\in\hat{\Omega}_{\eta,r}. Given t∈𝒯i​jt\in\mathcal{T}_{ij}, let η∼t\eta\sim t if j∼ηj\sim\eta and η\eta contains the side of tt opposite to jj.

Then:

Lemma 6.6.

Let i,j∈Ω^i,j\in\hat{\Omega}. Let t∈𝒯i​jt\in\mathcal{T}_{ij} and η=(i,k2,k3,…,kd)\eta=(i,k_{2},k_{3},\dots,k_{d}) be a pinning in Ω^i\hat{\Omega}_{i} such that j∼ηj\sim\eta and η∼t\eta\sim t. Then, there exist constants C,c>0C,c>0 such that if nn is sufficiently large then

∑x∈Ωη​j,y∈Ωη|ϕi​j,x​y|​π​(x)​P​(x,y)≤C​logc⁡n​ui​(t)Δ⋅π^​(η)​π^​(j).\sum_{x\in\Omega_{\eta j},y\in\Omega_{\eta}}|\phi_{ij,xy}|\pi(x)P(x,y)\leq\frac{C\log^{c}n\sqrt{u_{i}(t)}}{\Delta}\cdot\hat{\pi}(\eta)\hat{\pi}(j)\,.
Proof.

Let x∗x^{*} denote the dual tree of a given triangulation xx. Let xt∗x_{t}^{*} denote the subtree of x∗x^{*} rooted at the node corresponding to the triangle tt. Consider a breadth-first partitioning of the non-root nodes in xt∗x_{t}^{*} into levels L1,L2,…,LdL_{1},L_{2},\dots,L_{d} where we set d≤C′​(logc′⁡ui​(t))⋅ui​(t)d\leq C^{\prime}(\log^{c^{\prime}}u_{i}(t))\cdot\sqrt{u_{i}(t)} is either the maximum level in xt∗x_{t}^{*}, or C′​(logc′⁡ui​(t))⋅ui​(t)C^{\prime}(\log^{c^{\prime}}u_{i}(t))\cdot\sqrt{u_{i}(t)}, whichever is smaller. (We defer the choice of C′,c′C^{\prime},c^{\prime} for now.) Identify each node with the neighbor yy of xx obtained by performing a rotation at the edge connecting the node to its parent. By assumption j∼ηj\sim\eta (and therefore j∉ηj\notin\eta) let ϕ^=ϕi​j,η​j\hat{\phi}=\phi_{ij,\eta j}. By Lemma 5.10 and by applying induction to Lemma 6.2 we obtain ϕ^=ϕi​j,η​j=π^​(j)π^η​(j)\hat{\phi}=\phi_{ij,\eta j}=\frac{\hat{\pi}(j)}{\hat{\pi}_{\eta}(j)} and ∑y∈Lt|ϕi​j,x​y|≤π^​(j)π^η​(j)\sum_{y\in L_{t}}|\phi_{ij,xy}|\leq\frac{\hat{\pi}(j)}{\hat{\pi}_{\eta}(j)}. Therefore letting L⁡(y)L(y) denote the level of yy we have

𝔼x​𝔼y∼x​|ϕi​j,x​y|\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{x}\mathbb{E}_{y\sim x}|\phi_{ij,xy}| =𝔼x​[1Δ​∑y∼x|ϕi​j,x​y|]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{x}\left[\frac{1}{\Delta}\sum_{y\sim x}|\phi_{ij,xy}|\right]
=𝔼x[1Δ∑t=1d∑y∈Lt|ϕi​j,x​y|+1Δ∑y:L⁡(y)>d|ϕi​j,x​y|]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{x}\left[\frac{1}{\Delta}\sum_{t=1}^{d}\sum_{y\in L_{t}}|\phi_{ij,xy}|+\frac{1}{\Delta}\sum_{y:L(y)>d}|\phi_{ij,xy}|\right]
≤𝔼x​[1Δ​∑t=1dϕ^]+𝔼x​[1Δ​(# nodes at depth >d)⋅ϕ^]\displaystyle\leq\mathbb{E}_{x}\left[\frac{1}{\Delta}\sum_{t=1}^{d}\hat{\phi}\right]+\mathbb{E}_{x}\left[\frac{1}{\Delta}(\textnormal{\# nodes at depth }>d)\cdot\hat{\phi}\right]
=d​ϕ^Δ+𝔼x​[1Δ​(# nodes at depth >d)]⋅ϕ^\displaystyle=\frac{d\hat{\phi}}{\Delta}+\mathbb{E}_{x}\left[\frac{1}{\Delta}(\textnormal{\# nodes at depth }>d)\right]\cdot\hat{\phi}
≤d​ϕ^Δ+ui​(t)Δ⋅C′​logc′⁡(ui​(t))ui​(t)⋅ϕ^\displaystyle\leq\frac{d\hat{\phi}}{\Delta}+\frac{u_{i}(t)}{\Delta}\cdot\frac{C^{\prime}\log^{c^{\prime}}(u_{i}(t))}{\sqrt{u_{i}(t)}}\cdot\hat{\phi} (6.1)
≤C​logc⁡(ui​(t))⋅ui​(t)Δ⋅π^​(j)π^η​(j),\displaystyle\leq\frac{C\log^{c}(u_{i}(t))\cdot\sqrt{u_{i}(t)}}{\Delta}\cdot\frac{\hat{\pi}(j)}{\hat{\pi}_{\eta}(j)}\,, (6.2)

where we justify (6.1) as follows: if x∗x^{*} is a random tree and ν\nu is a random node in x∗x^{*} then by Lemma 6.3:

Pr[(depth of ν)>d]\displaystyle\Pr[(\textnormal{depth of }\nu)>d] ≤Pr[(depth of x∗)>d]\displaystyle\leq\Pr[(\textnormal{depth of }x^{*})>d]
≤C′n3/2exp(−d2/(4ui(t)))\displaystyle\leq C^{\prime}n^{3/2}\exp(-d^{2}/(4u_{i}(t)))
≤C′′n3/2exp(−(C′)2(log2​c′ui(t))/4)\displaystyle\leq C^{\prime\prime}n^{3/2}\exp(-(C^{\prime})^{2}\left(\log^{2c^{\prime}}u_{i}(t)\right)/4)
≤1ui​(t),\displaystyle\leq\frac{1}{\sqrt{u_{i}(t)}}\,,

whenever C′≥2C^{\prime}\geq\sqrt{2} and c′≥1/2c^{\prime}\geq 1/2.

Finally, the first claim follows from multiplying (6.2) by π^​(η​j)=π^​(η)​π^η​(j)\hat{\pi}(\eta j)=\hat{\pi}(\eta)\hat{\pi}_{\eta}(j). ∎

Lemma 6.7.

There exist constants C,c>0C,c>0 such that, for sufficiently large nn and for given i,j∈Ω^i,j\in\hat{\Omega} and t∈𝒯i​jt\in\mathcal{T}_{ij}, we have

∑η∼tπ^​(η)π⁡(Ωi​t)≤C​li​(t)​logc​n.\sum_{\eta\sim t}\frac{\hat{\pi}(\eta)}{\pi(\Omega_{it})}\leq C\sqrt{l_{i}(t)}\log^{c}n\,.
Proof.

We compute

∑η∼tπ^​(η)π⁡(Ωi​t)\displaystyle\sum_{\eta\sim t}\frac{\hat{\pi}(\eta)}{\pi(\Omega_{it})} =∑x∈Ωi​t∑η∈Ω^i:j∼η,x∈Ωηπ⁡(x)π⁡(Ωi​t)\displaystyle=\sum_{x\in\Omega_{it}}\sum_{\eta\in\hat{\Omega}_{i}:j\sim\eta,x\in\Omega_{\eta}}\frac{\pi(x)}{\pi(\Omega_{it})}
=∑x∈Ωi​tπ⁡(x)π⁡(Ωi​t)(|{η∈Ω^i:j∼η,x∈Ωη}|)\displaystyle=\sum_{x\in\Omega_{it}}\frac{\pi(x)}{\pi(\Omega_{it})}\left(|\{\eta\in\hat{\Omega}_{i}:j\sim\eta,x\in\Omega_{\eta}\}|\right)
=∑x∈Ωi​tπ⁡(x)π⁡(Ωi​t)​dj​(x)\displaystyle=\sum_{x\in\Omega_{it}}\frac{\pi(x)}{\pi(\Omega_{it})}d_{j}(x)
≤C​li​(t)​logc⁡n,\displaystyle\leq C\sqrt{l_{i}(t)}\log^{c}n\,,

for constants C,cC,c. The last inequality is by Corollary 6.5 and by the observation that dj​(x)d_{j}(x) is bounded by the depth of the binary tree corresponding to the triangulation xx. ∎

In other words, summing the combined measure of all pinnings η\eta such that η​j\eta j is a valid pinning, overcounts many states xx, as each state belongs to multiple nested pinnings. Lemma 6.7 states that the factor of overcounting is O~​(n)\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{n}), because the expected depth of the nesting is O~​(n)\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{n}).

The following was observed in [EF23, MRS97] and follows from straightforward computations using Stirling’s approximation and the Catalan formulas:

Lemma 6.8 ([EF23, MRS97]).

There exist constants C1,C2>0C_{1},C_{2}>0 such that sufficiently large nn, the probability that a random triangulation of the convex n+2n+2-gon contains a given triangle with side lengths r,s,n+2−r−sr,s,n+2-r-s, where r≤n+22r\leq\frac{n+2}{2} and s≤n+22s\leq\frac{n+2}{2}, is bounded by

C1(r​s)3/2≤∑x∈Ω:x​ contains ​tπ(x)≤C2(r​s)3/2,\frac{C_{1}}{(rs)^{3/2}}\leq\sum_{x\in\Omega:x\textnormal{ contains }t}\pi(x)\leq\frac{C_{2}}{(rs)^{3/2}}\,,

recalling that π\pi is the uniform measure.

To simplify notation, we will write that ∑x∈Ω:x​ contains ​tπ(x)=Θ(1(r​s)3/2)\sum_{x\in\Omega:x\textnormal{ contains }t}\pi(x)=\Theta\left(\frac{1}{(rs)^{3/2}}\right) instead of stating the full inequality in Lemma 6.8. We now prove the following:

Lemma 6.9.

There exist constants C,c>0C,c>0 such that, if nn is sufficiently large, then given i,j∈Ω^i,j\in\hat{\Omega},

∑t∈𝒯i​jπ⁡(Ωi​t)​li​(t)​ui​(t)≤C​n​logc​n​π^​(i).\sum_{t\in\mathcal{T}_{ij}}\pi(\Omega_{it})\sqrt{l_{i}(t)}\sqrt{u_{i}(t)}\leq C\sqrt{n}\log^{c}n\hat{\pi}(i)\,.
Proof.

Each t∈𝒯i​jt\in\mathcal{T}_{ij} has three sides: one side has endpoint jj and another endpoint ww in the interval [i,j−1][i,j-1]. Another side has endpoint jj and another endpoint zz in the interval [j+1,n+1][j+1,n+1]. The third side has endpoints ww and zz, satisfying i≤w<j<z≤n+1i\leq w<j<z\leq n+1.

Assume that j−i≤n+2−i2j-i\leq\frac{n+2-i}{2}. (If j−i>n+2−i2j-i>\frac{n+2-i}{2} the proof will be symmetric.) Let r=j−wr=j-w.

Then:

  1. 1.

    if z−j≤n+2−i2z-j\leq\frac{n+2-i}{2} let s=z−js=z-j;

  2. 2.

    if z−j>n+2−i2z-j>\frac{n+2-i}{2} let s=n+2−i−z+ws=n+2-i-z+w and note s≤n+2−i2s\leq\frac{n+2-i}{2}.

(In case (ii) we are setting ss to be the length of the “bottom” side of tt.) In each case, applying Lemma 6.8 to the subpolygon bounded by the edge (i,n+1)(i,n+1) and containing jj, we have

π⁡(Ωi​t)π^​(i)=Θ⁡(1(r​s)3/2).\frac{\pi(\Omega_{it})}{\hat{\pi}(i)}=\Theta\left(\frac{1}{(rs)^{3/2}}\right)\,.

Furthermore, in the first case we have ui​(t)=max⁡{r,s}u_{i}(t)=\max\{r,s\} and li​(t)≤n+2−il_{i}(t)\leq n+2-i; in the second case we have ui​(t)≤n+2−iu_{i}(t)\leq n+2-i and li​(t)=sl_{i}(t)=s.

Therefore

∑t∈𝒯i​jπ⁡(Ωi​t)π^​(i)⋅li​(t)⋅ui​(t)\displaystyle\sum_{t\in\mathcal{T}_{ij}}\frac{\pi(\Omega_{it})}{\hat{\pi}(i)}\cdot\sqrt{l_{i}(t)}\cdot\sqrt{u_{i}(t)} ≤∑r=1j−iΘ⁡(1r3/2)​∑s=1rΘ⁡(1s3/2)​n+2−i​r\displaystyle\leq\sum_{r=1}^{j-i}\Theta\left(\frac{1}{r^{3/2}}\right)\sum_{s=1}^{r}\Theta\left(\frac{1}{s^{3/2}}\right)\sqrt{n+2-i}\sqrt{r}
+∑r=1j−iΘ(1r3/2)∑s=r+1(n+2−i)/2Θ(1s3/2)n+2−is\displaystyle\qquad+\sum_{r=1}^{j-i}\Theta\left(\frac{1}{r^{3/2}}\right)\sum_{s=r+1}^{(n+2-i)/2}\Theta\left(\frac{1}{s^{3/2}}\right)\sqrt{n+2-i}\sqrt{s}
+∑r=1j−iΘ(1r3/2)∑s=j−i−r+1(n+2−i)/2Θ(1s3/2)sn+2−i\displaystyle\qquad+\sum_{r=1}^{j-i}\Theta\left(\frac{1}{r^{3/2}}\right)\sum_{s=j-i-r+1}^{(n+2-i)/2}\Theta\left(\frac{1}{s^{3/2}}\right)\sqrt{s}\sqrt{n+2-i}
=O⁡(n​log⁡n).\displaystyle=O\left(\sqrt{n}\log n\right)\,.

To see the last asymptotic equality, we note that the first term is bounded by

O⁡(n​∑r=1n1r​∑s=1∞1s3/2)=O⁡(n​log⁡n),O\left(\sqrt{n}\sum_{r=1}^{n}\frac{1}{r}\sum_{s=1}^{\infty}\frac{1}{s^{3/2}}\right)=O(\sqrt{n}\log n),

where we used the fact that the harmonic series is bounded by O⁡(log⁡n)O(\log n) and the series ∑s1/s3/2\sum_{s}1/s^{3/2} converges. We bound the other terms similarly.

∎

Lemma 6.10.

In the notation used in Lemma 5.1, given x,y∈Ωix,y\in\Omega_{i}, if ϕi​j,x​y≠0\phi_{ij,xy}\neq 0 then there exists a pinning η=(k1=i,k2,…,kd)\eta=(k_{1}=i,k_{2},\dots,k_{d}) such that j∼ηj\sim\eta and such that x∈Ωη​jx\in\Omega_{\eta j} or y∈Ωη​jy\in\Omega_{\eta j}.

Proof.

Recall that we defined ϕi​j,x​y=ϕi​j,η​s​t\phi_{ij,xy}=\phi_{ij,\eta st} whenever x∈Ωη​s​tx\in\Omega_{\eta st} and y∈Ωη​t​sy\in\Omega_{\eta ts}. From the definition of ϕi​j,η​s​t\phi_{ij,\eta st} we have that ϕi​j,η​s​t=0\phi_{ij,\eta st}=0 (and therefore ϕi​j,x​y=0\phi_{ij,xy}=0) whenever j∉ηj\notin\eta and j≠sj\neq s and j≠tj\neq t. The claim follows. ∎

Lemma 6.11.

There exist constants C,c>0C,c>0 such that if nn is sufficiently large, for given i,j∈Ω^i,j\in\hat{\Omega}, we have:

∑x∈Ωi∑η:x∈Ωη​j∑y∈Ωi:y∼x|ϕi​j,x​y|Δπ(x)P(x,y)≤Cnlogcn⋅π^(i)π^(j).\sum_{x\in\Omega_{i}}\sum_{\eta:x\in\Omega_{\eta j}}\sum_{y\in\Omega_{i}:y\sim x}|\phi_{ij,xy}|\Delta\pi(x)P(x,y)\leq C\sqrt{n}\log^{c}n\cdot\hat{\pi}(i)\hat{\pi}(j)\,.
Proof.

Note that for each x∈Ωix\in\Omega_{i}, there exists a unique t∈𝒯i​jt\in\mathcal{T}_{ij} such that x∈Ωi​tx\in\Omega_{it}. Also, there exists a unique pinning η\eta such that x∈Ωη​jx\in\Omega_{\eta j}. Also if x∈Ωη​jx\in\Omega_{\eta j} then η∼t\eta\sim t. By Lemma 6.10 if x∈Ωη​jx\in\Omega_{\eta j} and y∈Ωiy\in\Omega_{i} and ϕi​j,x​y≠0\phi_{ij,xy}\neq 0 then y∈Ωηy\in\Omega_{\eta}. Therefore:

∑x∈Ωi∑η:x∈Ωη​j∑y∈Ωi:y∼x|ϕi​j,x​y|Δπ(x)P(x,y)\displaystyle\sum_{x\in\Omega_{i}}\sum_{\eta:x\in\Omega_{\eta j}}\sum_{y\in\Omega_{i}:y\sim x}|\phi_{ij,xy}|\Delta\pi(x)P(x,y) =∑t∈𝒯i​j∑η∼t∑x∈Ωη​j∑y∈Ωη:y∼x|ϕi​j,x​y|Δπ(x)P(x,y)\displaystyle=\sum_{t\in\mathcal{T}_{ij}}\sum_{\eta\sim t}\sum_{x\in\Omega_{\eta j}}\sum_{y\in\Omega_{\eta}:y\sim x}|\phi_{ij,xy}|\Delta\pi(x)P(x,y)
≤C′​logc′​n​∑t∈𝒯i​j∑η∼tπ^​(η)​π^​(j)​ui​(t)\displaystyle\leq C^{\prime}\log^{c^{\prime}}n\sum_{t\in\mathcal{T}_{ij}}\sum_{\eta\sim t}\hat{\pi}(\eta)\hat{\pi}(j)\sqrt{u_{i}(t)} (6.3)
≤C′′​logc′′​n​∑t∈𝒯i​jπ⁡(Ωi​t)​π^​(j)​li​(t)​ui​(t)\displaystyle\leq C^{\prime\prime}\log^{c^{\prime\prime}}n\sum_{t\in\mathcal{T}_{ij}}\pi(\Omega_{it})\hat{\pi}(j)\sqrt{l_{i}(t)}\sqrt{u_{i}(t)} (6.4)
≤C​logc​n⋅n​π^​(i)​π^​(j),\displaystyle\leq C\log^{c}n\cdot\sqrt{n}\hat{\pi}(i)\hat{\pi}(j)\,, (6.5)

where (6.3) is by Lemma 6.6, (6.4) is by Lemma 6.7, and (6.5) is by Lemma 6.9, and where C′,C′′,c′,c′′C^{\prime},C^{\prime\prime},c^{\prime},c^{\prime\prime} come from Lemma 6.6 and Lemma 6.7. ∎

We are now ready to prove Lemma 5.2:

Proof of Lemma 5.2.

We construct a transport flow from Ω⁡[S]\Omega[S] to Ω⁡[T]\Omega[T] where S,T⊆Ω^S,T\subseteq\hat{\Omega}. We will then bound ρ¯Ω⁡[S]\bar{\rho}_{\Omega[S]}.

Define the flow as follows: consider the flow function ϕi​j:{(x,y)∈(Ωi∪Ωj)2∣P⁡(x,y)>0}→ℝ\phi_{ij}:\left\{(x,y)\in(\Omega_{i}\cup\Omega_{j})^{2}\mid P(x,y)>0\right\}\rightarrow\mathbb{R} in Lemma 5.1. Construct a function ϕ:{(x,y)∈(ΩS∪ΩT)2∣P⁡(x,y)>0}→ℝ\phi:\left\{(x,y)\in(\Omega_{S}\cup\Omega_{T})^{2}\mid P(x,y)>0\right\}\rightarrow\mathbb{R} as follows:

Given x,y∈Ω⁡[S]∪Ω⁡[T]x,y\in\Omega[S]\cup\Omega[T] such that P⁡(x,y)>0P(x,y)>0, let ϕx,y=∑i∈S,j∈Tϕi​j,x​y\phi_{x,y}=\sum_{i\in S,j\in T}\phi_{ij,xy}.

(We may assume that S∩T=∅S\cap T=\emptyset: otherwise, for all i∈S∩Ti\in S\cap T, one may construct a trivial flow ϕi​i\phi_{ii} that sends zero flow across every edge between adjacent pairs of states in Ωi\Omega_{i}.)

The functions ϕS\phi_{S} and ϕT\phi_{T} together induce an Ω⁡[S]\Omega[S]-Ω⁡[T]\Omega[T] flow (satisfying the axioms in in Section 2.5): this flow simply results from the (edge-wise) sum of all the flows Γi→j\Gamma^{i\rightarrow j}, i∈S,j∈Ti\in S,j\in T. By Lemma 3.4 this implies the existence of a transport flow ΓS→T\Gamma^{S\rightarrow T} from Ω⁡[S]\Omega[S] to Ω⁡[T]\Omega[T].

By Lemma 6.1 the maximum congestion incurred by this flow is at most Δ\Delta.

Let C,cC,c be the constants in Lemma 6.11. We bound ρ¯Ω⁡[S]\bar{\rho}_{\Omega[S]} as follows:

2​ρ¯Ω⁡[S]\displaystyle 2\bar{\rho}_{\Omega[S]} =Δπ^​(S)​∑x∈ΩS,y∈ΩS∪ΩT|ϕx​y|​π​(x)​P​(x,y)\displaystyle=\frac{\Delta}{\hat{\pi}(S)}\sum_{x\in\Omega_{S},y\in\Omega_{S}\cup\Omega_{T}}|\phi_{xy}|\pi(x)P(x,y) (6.6)
≤Δπ^​(S)​∑i∈S∑x∈Ωi∑j∈T∑y∈Ωi∪Ωj|ϕi​j,x​y|​π​(x)​P​(x,y)\displaystyle\leq\frac{\Delta}{\hat{\pi}(S)}\sum_{i\in S}\sum_{x\in\Omega_{i}}\sum_{j\in T}\sum_{y\in\Omega_{i}\cup\Omega_{j}}|\phi_{ij,xy}|\pi(x)P(x,y)
=Δπ^​(S)​∑i∈S∑j∈T∑η=(k1=i,k2,…,kd),j∼η∑x∈Ωη​j,y∈Ωη|ϕi​j,x​y|​π​(x)​P​(x,y)\displaystyle=\frac{\Delta}{\hat{\pi}(S)}\sum_{i\in S}\sum_{j\in T}~\sum_{\eta=(k_{1}=i,k_{2},\dots,k_{d}),\atop j\sim\eta}~\sum_{x\in\Omega_{\eta j},y\in\Omega_{\eta}}|\phi_{ij,xy}|\pi(x)P(x,y)
+Δπ^​(S)∑i∈S,j∈T∑x∈Ωi,y∈Ωj|ϕi​j,x​y|π(x)P(x,y)\displaystyle\quad+\frac{\Delta}{\hat{\pi}(S)}\sum_{i\in S,j\in T}\sum_{x\in\Omega_{i},y\in\Omega_{j}}|\phi_{ij,xy}|\pi(x)P(x,y) (6.7)
≤C​n​logc⁡nπ^​(S)​∑i∈S,j∈Tπ^​(i)​π^​(j)+1π^​(S)​∑i∈S,j∈T|ϕi​j,i​j|​π^​(i)​π^i​(j)\displaystyle\leq\frac{C\sqrt{n}\log^{c}n}{\hat{\pi}(S)}\sum_{i\in S,j\in T}\hat{\pi}(i)\hat{\pi}(j)+\frac{1}{\hat{\pi}(S)}\sum_{i\in S,j\in T}|\phi_{ij,ij}|\hat{\pi}(i)\hat{\pi}_{i}(j) (6.8)
=C​n​logc⁡nπ^​(S)​∑i∈S,j∈Tπ^​(i)​π^​(j)+1π^​(S)​∑i∈S,j∈Tπ^​(i)​π^​(j)\displaystyle=\frac{C\sqrt{n}\log^{c}n}{\hat{\pi}(S)}\sum_{i\in S,j\in T}\hat{\pi}(i)\hat{\pi}(j)+\frac{1}{\hat{\pi}(S)}\sum_{i\in S,j\in T}\hat{\pi}(i)\hat{\pi}(j) (6.9)
=C​n​logc⁡n​π^​(T),\displaystyle=C\sqrt{n}\log^{c}n\hat{\pi}(T)\,, (6.10)

where the factor of 2 on the left-hand side of (6.6) is because by the definition of ϕ\phi we have ϕx​y=−ϕy​x\phi_{xy}=-\phi_{yx} and also because we have defined ρ¯Ω⁡[S]\bar{\rho}_{\Omega[S]} as the average congestion of a transport flow that sends positive flow in at most one direction across an edge (x,y)(x,y).

We have (6.7) by Lemma 6.10. For (6.8) we have applied Lemma 6.11; we have also applied the definition ϕi​j,x​y=ϕi​j,i​j\phi_{ij,xy}=\phi_{ij,ij}, and have used the identity

Δ​∑x∈Ωi,y∈Ωjπ⁡(x)​P​(x,y)=π^​(i)​π^i​(j),\Delta\sum_{x\in\Omega_{i},y\in\Omega_{j}}\pi(x)P(x,y)=\hat{\pi}(i)\hat{\pi}_{i}(j)\,,

which follows from definitions. We have (6.9) by the definition ϕi​j,i​j=π^​(j)π^i​(j)\phi_{ij,ij}=\frac{\hat{\pi}(j)}{\hat{\pi}_{i}(j)}.

The claim follows from (6.10). ∎

We now prove Lemma 4.8, the last ingredient in the proof of Theorem 1.1 given in Section 4:

Proof of Lemma 4.8.

It suffices to apply Lemma 5.2 with Ω(t,η)\Omega^{(t,\eta)} substituted for Ω\Omega and, for each kk, with SS substituted for S^k(t,η)\hat{S}_{k}^{(t,\eta)}, with TT substituted for Ω^(t,η)∖S\hat{\Omega}^{(t,\eta)}\setminus S, and with Ω⁡[S]\Omega[S] and Ω⁡[T]\Omega[T] substituted for SS and TT respectively. The result then follows from plugging in the bounds on ρ¯Ω⁡[S]\bar{\rho}_{\Omega[S]} and ρ¯Ω⁡[T]\bar{\rho}_{\Omega[T]} given by Lemma 5.2. ∎

Appendix A Multi-way Single-Commodity Flows (MSFs) and Transport Flows

In this section we make formalize some missing details from Section 3.

We also prove Lemma 4.5. More precisely, we show that the flow construction of [EF23] implies the functional inequalities in Lemma 4.5.

First, concerning the definition of transport flows given in Section 3, we justify our assertion that one can assume that a transport flow uses a given transition (x,y)(x,y) if and only if it does not use (y,x)(y,x):

Lemma A.1.

Given S,T⊆ΩS,T\subseteq\Omega, suppose Γ=ΓS→T\Gamma=\Gamma^{S\rightarrow T} is a transport flow from SS to TT, and suppose for some (x,y)∈Ω2(x,y)\in\Omega^{2} such that P⁡(x,y)>0P(x,y)>0 there exist distinct paths γ,γ′\gamma,\gamma^{\prime} such that (x,y)∈γ,(y,x)∈γ′(x,y)\in\gamma,(y,x)\in\gamma^{\prime}, and Γ⁡(γ)>0\Gamma(\gamma)>0 and Γ⁡(γ′)>0\Gamma(\gamma^{\prime})>0. Suppose without loss of generality that Γ⁡(γ)>Γ⁡(γ′)\Gamma(\gamma)>\Gamma(\gamma^{\prime}).

Then Γ\Gamma can be modified to obtain a distribution Γ′\Gamma^{\prime} in which Γ′​(γ′)=0\Gamma^{\prime}(\gamma^{\prime})=0, without introducing a new path that uses (y,x)(y,x).

Proof.

If (x,y)∈γ(x,y)\in\gamma and (y,x)∈γ′(y,x)\in\gamma^{\prime}, where γ\gamma has endpoints z,wz,w and γ′\gamma^{\prime} has endpoints z′,w′z^{\prime},w^{\prime}, then let γ⁡[z,x],γ⁡[z′,y′]\gamma[z,x],\gamma[z^{\prime},y^{\prime}] (respectively γ⁡[y,w],γ⁡[x,w′]\gamma[y,w],\gamma[x,w^{\prime}]) denote the segments of the paths γ,γ′\gamma,\gamma^{\prime} from zz to xx and z′z^{\prime} to yy (respectively from yy to ww and from xx to w′w^{\prime}). Then let γ′′\gamma^{\prime\prime} be the path obtained from concatenating γ⁡[z,x]\gamma[z,x] with γ′​[x,w′]\gamma^{\prime}[x,w^{\prime}] and let γ′′′\gamma^{\prime\prime\prime} be obtained from concatenating γ′​[z′,y]\gamma^{\prime}[z^{\prime},y] with γ⁡[y,w]\gamma[y,w]. Now define the distribution Γ′\Gamma^{\prime} as follows:

  1. 1.

    for all paths δ∉{γ,γ′,γ′′,γ′′′}\delta\notin\{\gamma,\gamma^{\prime},\gamma^{\prime\prime},\gamma^{\prime\prime\prime}\} let Γ′​(δ):=Γ⁡(δ)\Gamma^{\prime}(\delta):=\Gamma(\delta).

  2. 2.

    Let Γ′​(γ′):=0\Gamma^{\prime}(\gamma^{\prime}):=0.

  3. 3.

    Let Γ′​(γ):=Γ⁡(γ)−Γ⁡(γ′)\Gamma^{\prime}(\gamma):=\Gamma(\gamma)-\Gamma(\gamma^{\prime}).

  4. 4.

    Let Γ′​(γ′′):=Γ⁡(γ′′)+Γ⁡(γ′)\Gamma^{\prime}(\gamma^{\prime\prime}):=\Gamma(\gamma^{\prime\prime})+\Gamma(\gamma^{\prime}).

  5. 5.

    Let Γ′​(γ′′′):=Γ⁡(γ′′′)+Γ⁡(γ′)\Gamma^{\prime}(\gamma^{\prime\prime\prime}):=\Gamma(\gamma^{\prime\prime\prime})+\Gamma(\gamma^{\prime})

We readily obtain from the definition above that Γ′\Gamma^{\prime} is a transport flow from SS to TT, that γ′′,γ′′′\gamma^{\prime\prime},\gamma^{\prime\prime\prime} do not use (y,x)(y,x), and that Γ′​(γ′)=0\Gamma^{\prime}(\gamma^{\prime})=0 as desired.

∎

Applying Lemma A.1 iteratively to a transport flow Γ\Gamma, one obtains a transport flow with the desired property.

Inspired by the Ford-Fulkerson algorithm [FF56], we also prove Lemma 3.4, which allows us to pass from combinatorial flows to transport flows:

Proof of Lemma 3.4.

For convenience, we modify the construction by adding a special “source” vertex (state) ss and a special “sink” vertex tt. We add transitions (the probabilities are irrelevant for the present aim) for each z∈Sz\in S and for each w∈Tw\in T.

Now we view the SS-TT flow instead as an ss-tt flow, in which we use the additional transitions to route flow rom ss to SS and TT to tt. Assign capacities to the (directed) edges in the resulting flow network in which the capacity of a (directed) edge (x,y)(x,y) across which ϕ\phi sends positive flow is equal to ϕ⁡(x,y)\phi(x,y).

We construct the desired transport flow (collection of paths forming the distribution Γ=ΓS→T\Gamma=\Gamma^{S\rightarrow T}) in an iterative fashion, by defining a sequence of weight functions {wt∣t∈[T]}\{w_{t}\mid t\in[T]\} where TT is finite and will be described shortly. For every z∈S,w∈Tz\in S,w\in T and for every (simple) path γ\gamma in (Ω,P)(\Omega,P) from zz to ww, let w0​(γ)=0w_{0}(\gamma)=0.

We will maintain the invariant that for all t≥0t\geq 0 and for every edge (x,y)(x,y), we will have

∑γ∋(x,y)wt​(γ)−∑γ∋(y,x)wt​(γ)≤ϕ⁡(x,y)\sum_{\gamma\ni(x,y)}w_{t}(\gamma)-\sum_{\gamma\ni(y,x)}w_{t}(\gamma)\leq\phi(x,y)

Given t≥0t\geq 0, let an edge (x,y)(x,y) be tight at iteration tt if ∑γ∋(x,y)wt​(γ)−∑γ∋(y,x)wt​(γ)=ϕ⁡(x,y)\sum_{\gamma\ni(x,y)}w_{t}(\gamma)-\sum_{\gamma\ni(y,x)}w_{t}(\gamma)=\phi(x,y).

The process will stop at time TT, where we define TT to be the minimum tt such that for all z∈Sz\in S,

∑γ∋(s,z)wt​(γ)=∑z∈S∑x∼zϕ⁡(z,x)\sum_{\gamma\ni(s,z)}w_{t}(\gamma)=\sum_{z\in S}\sum_{x\sim z}\phi(z,x)

Note that this is equivalent to the condition that for all w∈Tw\in T,

∑γ∋(w,t)wt​(γ)=∑x∼wϕ⁡(x,w)\sum_{\gamma\ni(w,t)}w_{t}(\gamma)=\sum_{x\sim w}\phi(x,w)

Now, given t≥0t\geq 0, if t=Tt=T then the weight function wtw_{t} forms a transport flow Γ\Gamma from SS to TT, by the definition of a transport flow. (Here we drop s,ts,t and their incident edges.)

If t<Tt<T, then we claim that there exists some ss-tt path γ\gamma such that no edge in γ\gamma is tight. Then we can simply increase the weight of some such path until an edge on the path becomes tight, obtaining wt+1​(γ)>wt​(γ)w_{t+1}(\gamma)>w_{t}(\gamma).

To see the claim, suppose for a contradiction that every ss-tt path has a tight edge. Then the set of all tight edges in the flow network forms a cut, call it 𝒞\mathcal{C}. By the max-flow-min-cut theorem, the combined weight of the edges in this cut is at least equal to the maximum flow under ϕ\phi that ss sends to tt. That is:

∑(x,y)∈𝒞∑γ∋(x,y)wt​(γ)≥∑z∈S∑x∼zϕ⁡(z,x)\sum_{(x,y)\in\mathcal{C}}\sum_{\gamma\ni(x,y)}w_{t}(\gamma)\geq\sum_{z\in S}\sum_{x\sim z}\phi(z,x)

However, we also have

∑z∈S∑γ∋(s,z)wt(γ)=∑γ:γ​is an s-t pathwt(γ)≥∑(x,y)∈𝒞∑γ∋(x,y)wt(γ)\sum_{z\in S}\sum_{\gamma\ni(s,z)}w_{t}(\gamma)=\sum_{\gamma:\gamma\textnormal{is an s-t path}}w_{t}(\gamma)\geq\sum_{(x,y)\in\mathcal{C}}\sum_{\gamma\ni(x,y)}w_{t}(\gamma)

where the first equality is because every ss-tt path γ\gamma contains at least one edge (s,z)(s,z) for some z∈Sz\in S. The last inequality is because the right-hand side is a summation over all ss-tt paths containing cut edges, and the left-hand side is a summation over all ss-tt paths.

These two inequalities together imply that

∑z∈S∑γ∋(s,z)wt​(γ)≥∑z∈S∑x∼zϕ⁡(z,x)\sum_{z\in S}\sum_{\gamma\ni(s,z)}w_{t}(\gamma)\geq\sum_{z\in S}\sum_{x\sim z}\phi(z,x)

Since by construction the left-hand side never exceeds the right-hand side, this implies that t=Tt=T, a contradiction. ∎

In the remainder of this section, we build the required machinery for proving Lemma 4.5. To this end, we will use the artifice of a multi-way single-commodity flow (MSF) introduced and used in [EF23]:

Definition A.2 ([EF23]).

Given a graph G=(V,E)G=(V,E), define a multi-way single-commodity flow (MSF) problem as a tuple (S,T,σ,δ)(S,T,\sigma,\delta) where:

  • •

    S⊆VS\subseteq V is the set of source vertices

  • •

    T⊆VT\subseteq V is the set of sink vertices

  • •

    σ:S→ℝ≥0\sigma:S\rightarrow\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0} is the surplus function

  • •

    δ:T→ℝ≥0\delta:T\rightarrow\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0} is the demand function

We require that ∑s∈Sσ⁡(s)=∑t∈Tδ⁡(t)\sum_{s\in S}\sigma(s)=\sum_{t\in T}\delta(t).

It may be that σ\sigma (or δ\delta) is a constant function. In this case we will sometimes denote by σ\sigma (or δ\delta) the value σ⁡(v)\sigma(v) (or δ\delta).

Definition A.3.

Given a graph G=(V,E)G=(V,E), let A=⋃{u,v}​i​n​E(u,v),(v,u)A=\bigcup_{\{u,v\}inE}{(u,v),(v,u)} be the set of directed arcs obtained by creating two copies of each (undirected) edge in EE, one copy in each direction.

Given an MSF problem Π=(S,T,σ,δ)\Pi=(S,T,\sigma,\delta) where S,T⊆VS,T\subseteq V, say that a function ϕ:A→ℝ\phi:A\rightarrow\mathbb{R} solves Π\Pi if ϕ\phi satisfies the following conditions:

  • •

    for all s∈S∖Ts\in S\setminus T, ∑u∈Vϕ⁡(s,u)=σ⁡(s)\sum_{u\in V}\phi(s,u)=\sigma(s)

  • •

    for all t∈T∖St\in T\setminus S, ∑u∈Vϕ⁡(u,s)=σ⁡(T)\sum_{u\in V}\phi(u,s)=\sigma(T)

  • •

    for all v∈S∩Tv\in S\cap T, ∑u∈Vϕ⁡(v,u)=σ⁡(v)−δ⁡(v)\sum_{u\in V}\phi(v,u)=\sigma(v)-\delta(v)

  • •

    for all v∈V∖(S∪T)v\in V\setminus(S\cup T), ∑u∈Vϕ⁡(v,u)=0\sum_{u\in V}\phi(v,u)=0

Call ϕ\phi a multi-way single-commodity flow (MSF), or simply a flow function.

Remark A.4.

To make our proofs more convenient, we have deviated from the definition of an MSF in [EF23], in that we define ϕ⁡(x,y)=−ϕ⁡(y,x)\phi(x,y)~=~-\phi(y,x), and when ϕ⁡(x,y)≥0\phi(x,y)\geq 0 we consider ϕ⁡(x,y)\phi(x,y) to denote the flow routed across the edge (x,y)(x,y) in the (x,y)(x,y) direction. We have adjusted the criteria for ϕ\phi accordingly in Definition A.3.

[EF23] instead considered the flow across the edge to be ϕ⁡(x,y)−ϕ⁡(y,x)\phi(x,y)-\phi(y,x) when ϕ⁡(x,y)≥ϕ⁡(y,x)\phi(x,y)\geq\phi(y,x).

[EF23] considered the problem of constructing a multicommodity flow in the graph (Ω,Q)(\Omega,Q) where Ω\Omega is the state space of the triangulation walk, viewed as the vertex set of a graph, and where Q={(x,y)∣P⁡(x,y)>0}Q=\{(x,y)\mid P(x,y)>0\} is the (undirected) edge set obtained by connecting every pair of triangulations x,y∈Ωx,y\in\Omega for which the transition probability P⁡(x,y)P(x,y) is nonzero. This graph is regular and unweighted (since π\pi is uniform and since all nonzero transition probabilities under PP are the same), and has degree Δ=n−1\Delta=n-1.

[EF23] considered a collection of MSF problems {Πs∣s∈Ω¯}\{\Pi_{s}\mid s\in\overline{\Omega}\} where

Πs=(Ωs,Ω,σ=1,δ=π¯​(s))\Pi_{s}=\left(\Omega_{s},\Omega,\sigma=1,\delta=\overline{\pi}(s)\right)

[EF23] decomposed Ω\Omega recursively according to the projection chain (Ω¯,P¯)(\overline{\Omega},\overline{P}) and the Cartesian product structure of each Ωs\Omega_{s} subspace, as we have done in Section 5.1. They showed that to construct a uniform multicommodity flow in (Ω,Q)(\Omega,Q), it suffices to construct an MSF for every Πt\Pi_{t} problem, for each projection graph (Ω¯,Q¯)(\overline{\Omega},\overline{Q}) that occurs at every level of the decomposition.

As our present aim is to prove Lemma 4.5, we wish to bound the variance

Varπ¯⁡F\displaystyle\operatorname{Var}_{\overline{\pi}}F =∑s∈Ω¯π¯​(s)​(F⁡(s)−𝔼π¯​F)2\displaystyle=\sum_{s\in\overline{\Omega}}\overline{\pi}(s)(F(s)-\mathbb{E}_{\overline{\pi}}F)^{2}
=∑s∈Ω¯π¯​(s)​(F⁡(s)−F⁡(Ω))2\displaystyle=\sum_{s\in\overline{\Omega}}\overline{\pi}(s)(F(s)-F(\Omega))^{2}

where we let F⁡(Ω)=𝔼π¯​F=𝔼π​fF(\Omega)=\mathbb{E}_{\overline{\pi}}F=\mathbb{E}_{\pi}f.

We consider the term π¯​(s)​(F⁡(s)−F​(Ω)2CLOSE\overline{\pi}(s)(F(s)-F(\Omega)^{2} to represent the problem of distributing π¯​(s)\overline{\pi}(s) total flow, initially concentrated evenly among the states in Ωs\Omega_{s}, throughout all of Ω\Omega.

That is, we associate the expression with the MSF problem Πs\Pi_{s}.

The following lemmas are implicit in [EF23] and immediate from the definitions. These lemmas connect MSFs with transport flows:

Lemma A.5.

Suppose an MSF problem Π=(S,T,σ,δ)\Pi=(S,T,\sigma,\delta) “decomposes” as a “serial” collection of problems

{Πk=(Sk,Tk,σk,δk)∣k∈[K]}\{\Pi_{k}=(S_{k},T_{k},\sigma_{k},\delta_{k})\mid k\in[K]\}

for some K≥1K\geq 1. That is, suppose for k∈[K−1]k\in[K-1], Tk=Sk+1T_{k}=S_{k+1} and δk=σk+1\delta_{k}=\sigma_{k+1}. Suppose S=S1S=S_{1} and T=TKT=T_{K}, and suppose σ=σ1\sigma=\sigma_{1} and δ=δK\delta=\delta_{K}.

Then σ​π​(S)=δ​π​(T)=σk​π​(Sk)=δk​π​(Tk)\sigma\pi(S)=\delta\pi(T)=\sigma_{k}\pi(S_{k})=\delta_{k}\pi(T_{k}) for all kk, and

σ​π​(S)​(f⁡(S)−f⁡(T))=∑kσk​π​(Sk)​(f⁡(Sk)−f⁡(Tk))=∑kδk​π​(Tk)​(f⁡(Sk)−f⁡(Tk))\sigma\pi(S)(f(S)-f(T))=\sum_{k}\sigma_{k}\pi(S_{k})(f(S_{k})-f(T_{k}))=\sum_{k}\delta_{k}\pi(T_{k})(f(S_{k})-f(T_{k}))
Lemma A.6.

Suppose an MSF problem (S,T,σ,δ)(S,T,\sigma,\delta) decomposes as a “parallel,” disjoint “composition” of problems

{Πk=(Sk,Tk,σk,δk)∣k∈[K]}\{\Pi_{k}=(S_{k},T_{k},\sigma_{k},\delta_{k})\mid k\in[K]\}

for some K≥1K\geq 1.

That is, suppose S=⋃k∈[K]SkS=\bigcup_{k\in[K]}S_{k} and T=⋃k∈[K]TkT=\bigcup_{k\in[K]}T_{k}. Suppose for k∈[K]k\in[K], for all s∈Sks\in S_{k}, σk​(s)=σ​(s)\sigma_{k}(s)=\sigma(s), and for all t∈Tkt\in T_{k}, δk​(t)=δ​(t)\delta_{k}(t)=\delta(t).

Then

σ​π​(S)=δ​π​(T)=∑kσk​π​(Sk)=∑kδk​π​(Tk)\sigma\pi(S)=\delta\pi(T)=\sum_{k}\sigma_{k}\pi(S_{k})=\sum_{k}\delta_{k}\pi(T_{k})
Corollary A.7.

If an MSF problem decomposes into (parallel, disjoint) sums and (serial) decompositions of problems {Πk=(Sk,Tk,σk,δk)}\{\Pi_{k}=(S_{k},T_{k},\sigma_{k},\delta_{k})\} such that the longest serial “chain” in the decomposition has length LL, then

σ​π​(S)​(f⁡(S)−f⁡(T))2≤L​∑kσk​π​(Sk)​(f⁡(Sk)−f⁡(Tk))2\sigma\pi(S)(f(S)-f(T))^{2}\leq L\sum_{k}\sigma_{k}\pi(S_{k})(f(S_{k})-f(T_{k}))^{2} (A.1)
Proof.

From the definitions of parallel and serial decompositions, the expression f⁡(S)−f⁡(T)f(S)-f(T) on the left-hand side decomposes into an expectation of chains (or “paths”) of telescoping differences, where the longest chain has length LL. We obtain the right-hand side by applying the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality. ∎

Considering the inequality in Lemma 4.5, one can compare the left-hand side of Eq. A.1 with the expression π¯​(s)​(F⁡(s)−F⁡(Ω))2\overline{\pi}(s)(F(s)-F(\Omega))^{2}, letting σ=1,S=Ωs\sigma=1,S=\Omega_{s}, and T=ΩtT=\Omega_{t}. Our aim is to show an inequality of the form (A.1), where Sk=Sk(t,ω)S_{k}=S_{k}^{(t,\omega)} as in Lemma 4.5.

For convenience, we will define the additional notion. Consider a collection of MSF problems, 𝒫={P1,P2,…,Pk}\mathcal{P}=\{P_{1},P_{2},\dots,P_{k}\}. Define the multicommodity transport flow (MTF) problem {𝒮,𝒯,{σi∣i=1,…,k},{δi∣i=1,…,k}}\{\mathcal{S},\mathcal{T},\{\sigma_{i}\mid i=1,\dots,k\},\{\delta_{i}\mid i=1,\dots,k\}\} where 𝒮={S1,…,Sk},𝒯={T1,…,Tk}\mathcal{S}=\{S_{1},\dots,S_{k}\},\mathcal{T}=\{T_{1},\dots,T_{k}\}. We say that a flow function ϕ={ϕi∣i=1,…,k}\phi=\{\phi_{i}\mid i=1,\dots,k\} solves the MTF 𝒫\mathcal{P} if ϕi\phi_{i} solves PiP_{i} for all ii.

We can then reason about subproblems (decomposition) of an MTF the way we do about an MSF: suppose MSF problems P=(S,T,σ,δ),P′=(S′,T′,σ′,δ′)P=(S,T,\sigma,\delta),P^{\prime}=(S^{\prime},T^{\prime},\sigma^{\prime},\delta^{\prime}) each split serially into P1=(S1,T1,σ1,δ1),P2=(S2,T2,σ2,δ2),P1′=(S1′,T1′,σ1′,δ1′),P2′=(S2′,T2′,σ2′,δ2′)P_{1}=(S_{1},T_{1},\sigma_{1},\delta_{1}),P_{2}=(S_{2},T_{2},\sigma_{2},\delta_{2}),P^{\prime}_{1}=(S^{\prime}_{1},T^{\prime}_{1},\sigma^{\prime}_{1},\delta^{\prime}_{1}),P^{\prime}_{2}=(S^{\prime}_{2},T^{\prime}_{2},\sigma^{\prime}_{2},\delta^{\prime}_{2}) and suppose T1=S2=T1′=S2′T_{1}=S_{2}=T^{\prime}_{1}=S^{\prime}_{2}. Then we consider the MTF problem 𝒫={P,P′}\mathcal{P}=\{P,P^{\prime}\} to be equivalent to the collection of MTF problems 𝒬={P1,P1′},ℛ={P2,P2′}\mathcal{Q}=\{P_{1},P^{\prime}_{1}\},\mathcal{R}=\{P_{2},P^{\prime}_{2}\}.

That is:

Remark A.8.

If an MTF problem 𝒫\mathcal{P} can be decomposed as in Eq. A.1, then the inequality in Eq. A.1 holds for 𝒫\mathcal{P}.

Lemma A.9 ([EF23a]).

Consider an MTF problem 𝒫\mathcal{P} (over the state space Ω\Omega) induced by |Ω¯||\overline{\Omega}| MSF problems {Pt∣t∈Ω¯}\{P_{t}\mid t\in\overline{\Omega}\} in which each central-triangle-induced class t∈Ω¯t\in\overline{\Omega} begins with a surplus σ=1\sigma=1, i.e. 𝒫t={S=Ωt,T=Ω,σ=1,δ=π¯​(t)}\mathcal{P}_{t}=\{S=\Omega_{t},T=\Omega,\sigma=1,\delta=\overline{\pi}(t)\}. There exists an MTF ϕ\phi that solves all of the problems {𝒫t}\{\mathcal{P}_{t}\} in which each edge in P¯\overline{P} carries total congestion at most O~​(n)\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{n}).

The maximum path length of ϕ\phi is O~​(1)\widetilde{O}(1).

Furthermore, 𝒫\mathcal{P} is equivalent to a collection of MTF subproblems each of which is of one of two forms:

  1. 1.

    𝒫t,t′=(Ωt​t′,Ωt′​t,σt​t′,δt​t′)\mathcal{P}_{t,t^{\prime}}=(\Omega_{tt^{\prime}},\Omega_{t^{\prime}t},\sigma_{tt^{\prime}},\delta_{tt^{\prime}}) where σt​t′=O~​(n)\sigma_{tt^{\prime}}=\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{n}).

  2. 2.

    𝒫t,k={(Sk(t,η),Ωt,σk,δk)}\mathcal{P}_{t,k}=\{(S_{k}^{(t,\eta)},\Omega_{t},\sigma_{k},\delta_{k})\} or 𝒫t,k={(Ωt,Sk(t,η),σk,δk)}\mathcal{P}_{t,k}=\{(\Omega_{t},S_{k}^{(t,\eta)},\sigma_{k},\delta_{k})\} where Sk(t,η)=⋃i∈SΩt​i(η)S_{k}^{(t,\eta)}=\bigcup_{i\in S}\Omega_{ti}^{(\eta)} for some S⊆Ω^(t,η)S\subseteq\hat{\Omega}^{(t,\eta)}, where η∈Ωt(1)×Ωt(2)\eta\in\Omega_{t}^{(1)}\times\Omega_{t}^{(2)} or η∈Ωt(2)×Ωt(3)\eta\in\Omega_{t}^{(2)}\times\Omega_{t}^{(3)} or η∈Ωt(1)×Ωt(3)\eta\in\Omega_{t}^{(1)}\times\Omega_{t}^{(3)} and where σk=O~​(n)\sigma_{k}=\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{n}).

Each tt participates in at most O~​(1)\widetilde{O}(1) of the subproblems.

Proof.

The series of lemmas in [EF23a, Appendix B] describes a collection of MSF problems (essentially an MTF problem) as described in the statement of this lemma, and establishes a flow construction with the congestion claimed. The construction decomposes 𝒫\mathcal{P} into subproblems of the two forms claimed: this is immediate from the proofs of [EF23a, Lemma 32, Lemma 38, Corollary 39, Lemma 40, and Lemma 41]. ∎

By Remark A.8, combining Lemma A.9 (in particular the bounds on the congestion and the maximum path length) with Eq. A.1 implies Lemma 4.5.

Lemma B.1 states that the congestion is monotonic as one travels around the polygon. See Fig. 12.

Proof of Lemma 6.1.

This analysis will closely follow [EF23].

We will prove by induction on |η||\eta| that for all η,\eta, |ϕη|≤1|\phi_{\eta}|\leq 1, implying the result—where we define ϕη:=∑i∈S,j∈Tϕi​j,η\phi_{\eta}:=\sum_{i\in S,j\in T}\phi_{ij,\eta}.

It will be helpful to observe that ϕ⋅,⋅\phi_{\cdot,\cdot} satisfies the axioms of a flow function. We wish to show that at most one unit of flow is sent across any x,yx,y edge.

Observe first that for all η=i∈Ω^\eta=i\in\hat{\Omega}, and for all s∈Ω^i,ls\in\hat{\Omega}_{i,l} (similarly s∈Ω^i,rs\in\hat{\Omega}_{i,r}) each triangulation in Ωη​s=Ωi​s\Omega_{\eta s}=\Omega_{is} can be viewed as having at most one unit of congestion that it may have received from a neighboring state in some Ωs​i\Omega_{si} (if s∈Ts\in T), and which it must distribute throughout Ωη\Omega_{\eta}, i.e.

ϕη​s=∑j∈Tϕi​j,η​s=ϕs,η​s\phi_{\eta s}=\sum_{j\in T}\phi_{ij,\eta s}=\phi_{s,\eta s}

and therefore |ϕη​s|≤1|\phi_{\eta s}|\leq 1.

Then for all s,t∼ηs,t\sim\eta we have

ϕη​s​t\displaystyle\phi_{\eta st} =∑j∈Tϕi​j,η​s​t\displaystyle=\sum_{j\in T}\phi_{ij,\eta st} (B.12)
=∑j∈Tπ^η​(t)π^η​s​(t)​(ϕi​j,η​t−ϕi​j,η​s)\displaystyle=\sum_{j\in T}\frac{\hat{\pi}_{\eta}(t)}{\hat{\pi}_{\eta s}(t)}(\phi_{ij,\eta t}-\phi_{ij,\eta s}) (B.13)
=π^η​(t)π^η​s​(t)​(∑j∈Tϕi​j,η​t−∑j∈Tϕi​j,η​s)\displaystyle=\frac{\hat{\pi}_{\eta}(t)}{\hat{\pi}_{\eta s}(t)}(\sum_{j\in T}\phi_{ij,\eta t}-\sum_{j\in T}\phi_{ij,\eta s}) (B.14)

and applying Lemma 5.4 and Lemma B.1 implies |ϕη​s​t|≤1|\phi_{\eta st}|\leq 1. ∎
